subtopic: SOFTWOOD LUMBER PRODUCTS EXPORT CHARGE ACT

speechtext:
The House resumed from Monday, January 19, consideration of the motion of Miss Carney that Bill C-37, an Act respecting the imposition of a charge on the export of certain softwood lumber products, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee, and the amendment of Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra), (p. 2393).
Hon. Gerald S. Merrithew (Minister of State (Forestry and
Mines)): Mr. Speaker, I am delighted today to be able to put some facts on the record in this particular debate which has been sometimes clouded by some misperceptions and halftruths. It is an important debate for Canada, I agree. We have been working at it for a long time. Of course, the whole issue of our softwood trade has been one which has been most prolonged. It is not new at all. It has gone on for decades and decades. I have been part of it for four or five years. It is perhaps one of the most bitter disputes in the history of Canada-U.S. trade relations.
Since the Memorandum of Understanding reached with the United States on December 30, we have put behind us a lot of difficult negotiations with the U.S. It seems to me we are now in a position to strengthen our industry without the constant threat of other trade irritants. We can now try to be competitive in a a very competitive market. I do not have to emphasize how divisive this issue has been to our national fabric. It would be extremely unfortunate if the degree of rancour and mistrust which so characterized our negotiations with the United States carried forward within Canada as we proceed to implement the agreement and to examine alternative provincial measures in the export charge.
It is necessary for Canada to unite and find a realistic and effective solution to the challenges with which we are faced. Indeed, the federal Government has been very conscious of the need to remain united in dealing with this very bitter dispute with the United States. A high level of goodwill and a spirit of co-operation characterized our discussion with the provinces last week in Vancouver and some of the comments I have heard recently from the industry have been more positive and helpful than the initial reaction to the agreement by some industry spokesmen.
The workers in British Columbia and elsewhere in Canada who have such an important stake in the outcome of this dispute have been very supportive of our efforts to secure an understanding with the United States. Sadly, I have also heard
January 20, 1987

comments from the Opposition who, in many instances, have taken this opportunity as a means to achieve their own personal political objectives. It is unfortunate to see the great divergence of opinion between certain members of the Opposition and those to whom they perceive to be their own constituency. It must be extremely frustrating for the New Democratic Party to find so few people in the labour movement who oppose the initiative of the Government to secure an understanding with the United States. Many of the provincial wings of that same Party have come out in support of a negotiated settlement. For example, the British Columbia forestry critic has called the softwood lumber deal agreement a pretty good deal.
As for the Official Opposition, I find it ironic to hear those Hon. Members even talking about forestry. For almost two decades that Party presided over the dissemination of the federal Government's forestry service and the downgrading of the leadership role of the federal Government in this key sector of our economy. Its lack of commitment to forestry is a matter of public record. The forest community already knows and recognizes this. It is regrettable it has taken this situation to raise the interest of that Party. However, I laud Members of the Liberal Party for now taking a keener interest in forestry and call upon them and other members of the Opposition to put their rancour aside in order to make this agreement work on behalf of all Canadians. The development of the forest industry is too important to the economy of this country to be subject to shabby theatrics and partisan politics.
I would like now to turn my attention to some of the specifics of the understanding with the United States. The critics have been less than objective in their statements in the softwood lumber dispute. They have consistently ignored the realities of that dispute and the real options which were available to the Government, in fact, all Governments of Canada. The critics imply that the choice was between an agreement with the United States or continuing free trade in lumber. The real choice was not that. It was between a countervailing duty or other restrictive measures imposed unilaterally by the United States against Canadian softwood lumber exports or a negotiated settlement. In other words, a punitive countervail or an agreement by choice. The Government could have chosen to fight to the bitter end. This would not have served Canadian interests. To ignore the political realities of the issue would have deprived us of any control over the situation. The choice was between having the Americans tax our lumber or our agreeing to tax it ourselves. This has been entirely overlooked by the critics.
For the benefit of the House, I would like to review the three objectives which were set out by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the nine Premiers at the First Ministers' Conference in Vancouver in November. Basically, they wanted us to protect Canadian sovereignty, second, to avoid a precedent in U.S. trade law which would be damaging to Canadian interests and, third, they wanted us to keep the money in Canada. In our negotations we stood fast. Our
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
negotiators held on to Canada's position right to the very end. We have met all three of those objectives.
Let us examine those objectives in turn. First, the softwood lumber agreement respects and maintains our sovereignty and avoids the intrusion by the United States into Canadian affairs which would have occurred with a countervailing duty action. As a former Minister responsible for forestry in New Brunswick, I understand the importance of being fully in control with respect to how we manage our forestry resource for the betterment of our citizens. Under the agreement, the export charges were set at an agreed level, 15 per cent. A countervailing duty could be unilaterally raised by the United States following an annual review. That would be unacceptable. Under the agreement, Canada administers the export charge and monitors its effect and is required only to provide the information to the United States. A countervailing duty, on the other hand, would be subject to actual policing by the United States. Under the agreement, Canada is free to replace the export charge with stumpage increases or other measures at a time and level of our own chosing. Only the value of these changes is subject to consultation and agreement with the United States. A countervailing duty, on the other hand, would have severely limited Canada's freedom of action. The timing, the nature and the value of any replacement measures would have been unilaterally determined by the Americans.
Suggestions by the Opposition that our sovereignty has been threatened by this agreement are completely without foundation. Any student of international politics knows that bilateral agreements between nations involve, in some way, an intrusion into the other's business, be it a quota, a normal commercial transaction or a verification clause. There is far less intrusion into Canada's forest management policies under this agreement than there would have been with a countervailing duty.
The second objective was to avoid a highly damaging precedent that could have affected other exports to the United States. I remind Hon. Members that the basic issue involved here is whether or not the policies of Canadian Governments, in managing and pricing their own natural resources, could be subject to the trade remedy legislation of other nations. Under this agreement which we negotiated and signed on December 30 the dangerous legal precedent set by the unfavourable preliminary determination made by the U.S. Government in the softwood lumber case last October has been nullified. A countervailing duty would have confirmed that precedent and left Canada more vulnerable to similar actions against other resource exports.
The third objective was to ensure that the money remained in Canada, for Canadians, and did not become a contribution to the United States Treasury. Under the agreement the provinces are free to use the revenues from the export charge to replenish our forests, to provide adjustment assistance for affected workers, to assist our forest industry in developing alternative markets abroad, or to advance the development of

January 20, 1987
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
new technologies. Under a countervailing duty action these Canadian funds would have gone directly into the Treasury of the United States, and would not have been available to create jobs and to lessen the negative impact on affected workers and communities.
While it is still much too early to predict the full impact of the export charge on the Canadian lumber industry, it is clear that some export sales to the U.S., and jobs, will be lost. The degree to which these adverse effects occur across the country largely depends on how much of the duty can be passed on to the U.S. consumer-and it appears a good deal of it has been to date-and the supply response of the American producers. Early indications show that a substantial portion of the export charge is now being borne by the U.S. consumer. We will continue to monitor this situation.
Nevertheless, the point I am making is that as a result of our negotiations the provinces have the financial resources to respond to this situation. In the area of forest management it is our estimation that over 100,000 jobs, both direct and indirect, will be created during the life of the forestry development agreements negotiated with the provinces. At the same time this ensures a long term timber supply. These forest development agreements have a price-tag of $1.1 billion of federal and provincial contributions. I wish to mention that is a 400 per cent increase since the time the Liberals governed our country.
I again want to reiterate my call for pulling together on this issue. This will be extremely important as we examine possible replacement measures in whole or in part, such as stumpage increases, to the export charge. As a result of our meeting in Vancouver last week, Canada's provincial and federal Ministers responsible for forestry have agreed to address this issue in more detail. I can assure the House that both myself and my provincial counter-parts place considerable importance on involving businessmen and labour in this process. The issues involved are very complex. We will not be stampeded into any quick-fix solutions that are not in the over-all interests of Canada.
My colleagues and I will be having our initial meeting on the issue of replacement measures during the next Canadian Council of Forest Ministers meeting to take place in Montreal on January 26. I have been encouraged by the collective and the unanimous desire of the provincial Forestry Ministers to work co-operatively since the Council was established in 1985. We have co-operated on a great many issues, and I am sure we can co-operate on this very difficult issue which we have now undertaken. Each and every provincial Minister is committed, as am I, to co-operating with all parties in the forest sector to move ahead to meet the challenges which still lie before us.

speechtext: Are there questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) indicated that from the very beginning the process included the co-operation of all the
players involved. I remember, as I am sure he will, time and time again when Members raised questions in the House with respect to how things were progressing in the United States in terms of the countervail case before the Department of Commerce and the ITC, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) asking members of the Opposition not to raise the issue in the House of Commons. We were told that everything was progressing well, that in co-operation with all of the players the Canadian Government was absolutely certain that the case Canada had put forward was iron-clad and that we had nothing to fear. Then October 21, after the Commerce Department brought in its preliminary ruling which found Canadian exports to be subsidized by 15 per cent, the Minister for International Trade, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney), said that we would fight it all the way. She said: "Today it's lumber. Tomorrow it could be any number of issues. We all agree that this ruling is deplorable, artificial and contrived and does not stand up to extensive analysis". She then went on to say that the United States' action "strikes directly at the sovereign right of a government to manage its own resources" and that negotiations would only condone the precedent. She said: "First we must fight to reverse this verdict".
The Minister for International Trade said that this move was a direct infringement on Canadian sovereignty. The Minister of State for Forestry says that is not the case. Will the Minister explain what the Minister for International Trade was saying on October 21 ?

subtopic: SOFTWOOD LUMBER PRODUCTS EXPORT CHARGE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very much part of those discussions when we talked of fighting the issue. I was part of the talks which we had in 1982 and in 1983 when we fought the previous countervailing duty issue which, incidentally, did not work. There has been some indication that it was won by either industry or by the Liberal Government. Unfortunately, within just a matter of months there was another case. So there was no winner in this particular case. At one point in time there was no question but that it was profitable for us to stick together. However, the political reality of what was happening in the United States and the rampant protectionist sentiments which were being expressed in the American Congress and in the industry dictated to us that the political situation had changed. As a result of intelligence we obtained from lawyers in the American industry, our government lawyers, our embassy staff and our friends in industry and government in the United States we were told that the handwriting was on the wall, that we could not win. The preliminary decision was already down against us and on October 16 it was negative to Canada.
What other choice did we have? There were but two. First, we could either continue to fight the issue through the courts and pay the money to the United States over the intervening period of time, or fight it in GATT. Or, second, we could try to negotiate a settlement. If one considers the facts of the matter, the result of negotiating a settlement Canada is by far ahead of the situation.

speechtext: I wish to address my question to the Minister. speechtext:
We were very much part of the debate which took place following the shakes and shingles issue in the House. We heard the doom and the gloom that the whole world was going to come to an end, shakes and shingles would be destroyed forever. The Opposition House Leader said that
10,000	jobs would be lost. There are only 4,000 such jobs in all of Canada. I do not know where he got his figures. The NDP indicated that the whole world would come to an end. In fact, very little has happened. The industry is now working near to capacity. We are being competitive. We know that the supply of red cedar in the United States will run out, and then we will be even more competitive. There was absolutely no truth to the fact that the world was going to come to an end because of the countervail on shakes and shingles.
Regarding the lumber issue, nobody in the country, certainly not in the Chamber, has any magic answers as to how many jobs will be lost. A lot will depend on how many of those jobs and what per cent of the cost will be absorbed by the American consumer. Quite frankly, it is my view, and it has been our indication to date, that the American consumer is the one who will be penalized. In the future we will know what effect there will be on our marginal mills, or the impacts on our domestic interprovincial markets. At this time I will not comment on that, because we do not know. It is proof positive by the type of irresponsible statements that were made following the shakes and shingles debate that at this time it is better not to hazard a guess. We will monitor that particular situation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to put on record some comments regarding Bill C-37, an Act respecting the imposition of a charge on the export of certain softwood lumber products to the United States, or we assume to the United States. We are still questioning whether under GATT we have the right to levy a special tax on one country and how other trading partners in the softwood industry will feel about it, whether or not they will take it to GATT and ask it to be applied to all countries which receive softwood exports from Canada.
However, it is appropriate to spend a moment or two to put the whole matter into some context today. We recognize that there is a $4 billion lumber export to the United States from Canada, representing nearly 15 billion board feet and 88 per cent of our total lumber exports. Obviously we are talking about the Canadian softwood export industry virtually in total.
It is useful for us as parliamentarians to recall that we are discussing the woods industry of Canada which employs,
directly and indirectly, 780,000 Canadians. It is a major aspect of the Canadian economy and of course the overwhelming leader in our trade.
Over the last number of years the Canadian lumber sector modernized and retooled its sawmills. It spent a great deal of money modernizing its operations. Of course, the high quality of SPF-spruce, pine, and fir-from Canada are recognized the world over to be extremely high quality lumber and sell in world markets at premium prices; people are prepared to pay more than the going rate to obtain first rate Canadian lumber. Our workers in the woods are extremely productive. They are among the most productive in the world. Consequently, it enabled the Canadian industry was able to expand significantly its exports to the United States over the last number of years. By and large the quality of wood there is significantly less. The mills are antiquated and outdated. They are still using big rip-saws which end up with excessive amounts of sawdust from sawn logs.
Quite frankly, we did such an excellent job in terms of our high productivity levels and our ability to compete internationally that we were able to send lumber from the northern parts of Canada down to the United States, to sell it in Tennessee, to take the Americans head on in the market-place, and to be successful.
When we add on transportation costs to our wood product delivery, it gives an idea of just how competitive and productive is the Canadian operation. It is first class, and we can be very proud of the sector.
The Americans recognized that they had to do something about their old-fashioned, antiquated operations, low productivity sector and poor quality lumber. A few years ago they set out to attempt to keep the Canadians out of their market and to increase their prices by keeping out Canadian competition. They lobbied their Congressmen and key Senators, such as Senator Baucus, Senator Gibbons, Senator Packwood, and others, and they did it successfully. They got Congress to take a number of initiatives which would in fact work against the Canadian interest in the United States.
Why they feel that Canadians having 35 per cent of their softwood market is inappropriate is beyond me, considering the percentages of various markets which they have in Canada-40 per cent, 50 per cent, 80 per cent and even 95 per cent in some sectors. However, they felt it was inappropriate for Canada to have 35 per cent of their softwood market and took the retaliatory actions of which we know so well over the last number of months.

The industry and the unions involved worked co-operatively and did an excellent job. They presented a good case and won. However, in the last little while that certainly has not been the case.

Reading from the standard text by Charles Fenwick, sovereignty means the repudiation of the right of a stronger state to intervene in the affairs of a weaker state. It has come to represent the will of smaller states to exist as separate and independent members of the international community.
That has always been Canada's assertion. We have a particular problem because we share a continent with the largest and most powerful country in the world. We recognize the need to maintain a balancing act between dealing properly with our friends and allies who share the continent and at the same time defending our independence and sovereignty. That is a balancing act and no one says it is easy. It has to be a central preoccupation of any Canadian Government and it has been over the years. We all know how important it is to make sure you do not shift the balance too far one way or the other.
We have recognized that one important way of ensuring that the balance is maintained is to establish, through the international community, rules which restrain the exercise of the power of the stronger state, whether it is on matters of the environment, defence or trade. Canadian regimes of all political stripes, Conservatives and Liberals, up until now have recognized that the best way to preserve and maintain that balancing act is to strengthen the international community, to put procedures in place where other countries of similar size and nature can help determine the rules. The Hon. Member knows that the whole mood of the United States is one of protectionism and of putting up barriers to international trade. He knows that is going on. He knows of the number of individual Bills which are being sponsored through Congress right now.
Thus the Government was faced with a difficult choice. We could either pay a countervail duty to the United States Treasury to the tune of $800 million per year, or even larger, and hope that we would win the case by following the rules. Over the next four years that would bring the total sum up to approximately $2.5 billion. We could have conceded the issue and suspended any action until Canada brought about offsetting measures, such as the imposition of a countervail duty. By doing that we would have started a trade war with our biggest trading partner. That is what we are talking about.
We are not talking about a dispute with a country on which we do not depend for a great deal of our trade. We are talking about a country which accounts for 75 per cent to 80 per cent of all our foreign trade.
The third option we had was that of negotiation. We could sit down and negotiate our way out of a mess which was created by a countervail duty without affecting other negotiations which were ongoing to secure access to markets. We could get out of the mess without setting a precedent that would affect other sectors of the economy. In other words we had to sit down like reasonable people and try to negotiate a solution to a very serious problem which affects a significant Canadian industry.
I have the impression as a result of listening to the Members of the NDP and the Liberal Party that we should not negotiate with the Americans. I am left with the impression that they think if we negotiate with them we will lose. They seem to say that we should fight, put up barriers and throw hand-grenades. And then when they do come out with a policy which may affect Canada we have to run to them and say: "You have to exempt us because we are one of your best friends". We cannot do that sort of thing.
So what did the Minister do? She instructed her officials and we moved in to negotiate an agreement. The federal Government did not move in to negotiate an agreement unilaterally. It did not go in as a centralist government and say: "We will negotiate". What the Government did is it went to the provinces, sat down with them and then brought them in on the negotiations. The approach they would dictate is defined by their going to the United States and sitting down with their counterparts to negotiate this agreement. There was co-operation all the way. As a result, nine provinces out of ten agreed with the final position taken. The one province which did not agree was the Province of Ontario. However, it will come onside when the issue is finally resolved.
What the softwood lumber dispute illustrates to all of us is just some of the trade problems faced by Canada and the U.S. It also demonstrates how essential it is for our two sovereign countries to get together and hammer out new rules to settle such disagreements. We cannot allow our trade position with the United States to deteriorate to a point that we will find these types of problems popping up every week or every second week. We have to put a system in place by which disputes of this nature can be solved in a reasonable manner, as was done with the lumber dispute.
I would also like to speak for a moment about the sovereignty issue which I think is very important. I believe that sovereignty is extremely important to all Canadians, just as it is extremely important to all Americans. We have heard members of the NDP and members of the Liberal Party talk about sovereignty and how it has been eroded as a result of our entering into a bilateral agreement with another country on a trade issue. What they fail to say, and most assuredly why they failed to say it is clear, is that when this country entered into
January 20, 1987

the GATT agreements we gave up, in a sense, some sovereignty or some decision making simply because we have agreed to abide by certain conditions. If we break those conditions then certain things will happen. We will lose our sovereignty in terms of being able to change the rules as we want because we have entered into an agreement.
Each time we enter into a bilateral agreement with any country on any trade issue, whether it be in the area of fisheries, hydro projects in British Columbia or in Quebec, or others, they are monitored by both countries. What members of the Opposition fail to say is that we also monitor bilateral agreements with the United States. We monitor what is going on in the United States. So in the truest sense I suppose that the United States also gives up some of its sovereignty. Through GATT we monitor events which are taking place in the United States, and the United States gives up some of its sovereignty. But that is not the issue. It is a red herring and Members opposite know that.
Let us look at some of the results of the agreement which has been entered into. The Coalition for Fair Lumber Imports is now withdrawing its petition which led to the countervail decision. As a consequence we are introducing legislation to impose a 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber, excluding all those small plants and companies which impose a value-added levy to the products they ship to the United States. The 15 per cent will not be imposed on those groups. The 15 per cent on the primary production of softwood lumber will be imposed as an export tax. The money from the export tax will go directly into the federal Government coffers. Rather than going into the United States coffers, it is now coming into the Canadian coffers.
The next part of the agreement with the provinces is that the money will be redirected to the provinces that are producing the softwood lumber and shipping it to the United States. They will be able to use it for reforestation, silviculture, or any displacement that may take place in the labour force. The key is that the provinces still control the resource, the federal Government does not.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry stated that we should have maintained what they did in 1982 or 1983. Yes, they acted. They were the ones who brought in the national energy policy and attacked the resources of the provinces. I suggest that if they were in Government today that they would be collecting the export duty and keeping it here in Ottawa. This Government is saying that the resources belong to the provinces and they are responsible. Therefore, the export tax that will be collected on exports to the United States will be redirected to the provinces, as it should be.
The agreement essentially maintains exemptions for exports of certain Canadian companies operating in British Columbia, Ontario, and Quebec, most of the producing provinces that do have value added to the lumber before it is shipped to the

United States. It will not apply to the value added in the remanufacturing process. That is a commitment that we have.
Most important is the argument we hear, "Gee, you entered into this agreement with the United States on the softwood lumber. My goodness, that will affect all other areas and every other agreement that we might want to develop or reach with the United States". The indications are very clear that this is not so. The proposal to the U.S. Government that was made between Canada and the United States on the softwood lumber was made without prejudice. Without prejudice means that this can never be used as an example of what was done before which can be used in another area. Without prejudice is a common term that lawyers use. They write a letter and put on it "without prejudice", which means that this agreement was drawn up without prejudice.
It is a good agreement. Certainly there will be cost. As the Members over there have clearly indicated, this cost will be passed on to the consumer in the United States. Indications are that the price of lumber has already gone up about 13 per cent in the United States and our sales from Canada to the United States should not be affected.
I rest my case, Mr. Speaker, and thank you for the opportunity.

maintopic: SEAL POPULATION GROWTH-DAMAGE COSTS SUFFERED BY FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one year ago I appeared before the Malouf Royal Commission on Sealing and outlined the serious costs associated with not arresting the growth of the seal population. Fishermen whom I represent are suffering because seals are damaging nets and traps, contributing to the spread of parasites, and consuming fish.
One seal consumes 3,200 pounds of fish annually. There are in excess of 100,000 grey seals consuming millions of pounds of fish each year off Atlantic Canada.
At a time of conservation of stocks and increasing emphasis on quality, millions of dollars worth of fish are being lost. The loss in terms of jobs is also substantial.
In my view the situation requires a seal cull as soon as possible. The issue is critically important to the Atlantic Canadian fishery and all of Atlantic Canada.

VIA RAIL

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the House the indignation and anger felt in western Canada with respect to the fact that VIA Rail was allowed to lay off all its Red Caps in western Canada while Red caps were kept on in major centres in eastern Canada. Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate you on permitting an exhibition of paintings by Canadian artist Armand Vallee in honour of Raoul Wallenberg, here in the House of Commons. He was in Hungary where it was his task to direct efforts to save Hungarian Jews from deportation to Nazi death camps.
Raoul Wallenberg showed tremendous courage and total disregard for his own safety by saving an estimated 100,000 Jewish men, women, and children. He has been kept prisoner in the Soviet Union since 1945, with reports insisting he is still alive. At that time we also encouraged the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to take all diplomatic steps necessary to secure his release.
I urge the Government to increase its efforts to save Raoul Wallenberg. This violation of human rights by the Soviet Union cannot be tolerated. We must show the Soviet Union that Canada has not and will not forget this hero to humanity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are almost 20,000 honey producers in Canada, nearly 5,000 of whom live on the Prairies. Unfortunately, like so many agricultural producers today, they are having a difficult time getting a fair price and establishing new markets for their honey.

TREATMENT OF PENSIONERS
speechtext:

RESIGNATION OF HON. MEMBER FOR YUKON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured today to rise along with my friends, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), and the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent), to pay a tribute to the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen).
His resignation was greeted with sadness on this side, and obvious relief on the other side. Erik Nielsen has known triumph and tragedy, attack and applause. None of these was able to distract him from his chosen course. He is one of the remaining Members of the small band who served with such distinction under the leadership of the late Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker in government and opposition, in good times and bad.
Words are inadequate tools to express the debt owed to Erik Nielsen by Parliament, by this Party, and by this country.
Occasionally the halls of Parliament bear witness to skill and dedication far beyond the normal. I will acknowledge that from time to time Erik was partisan. I owe him a special debt because I came into the House as a brand new Member never having been here before. I sat down over there, after walking in for the first time, not even knowing the sounds, and what have you. It is an intimidating experience to be here for the first time, and also to be here as Leader of a political Party. I had a few rough days or weeks in the process-very rough, in fact. One night I called my mother to ask her how I was doing. She said, "Brian, you are doing just great. You are doing fine. But when Mr. Nielsen says sit down, sit down."

Erik Nielsen as a parliamentarian is worthy to stand with the giants of the past. Those of us who had the good fortune to sit with him in the House must know that this was a man of no ordinary compass.
Hon. Erik Nielsen

He was fully devoted to the service of his country. He flew with the allied forces during World War II and upon his return from Europe he studied law and opened his own law office in Whitehorse.
His first election was controversial, and perhaps this was an indication of the kind of very tumultuous political career he was going to have. Throughout his 29 years on the parliamentary scene he has always been right where the action was-or certainly never far from it.

If there is one word characterizing Erik Nielsen's approach to life-irrespective of partisan differences-that word is duty. He made no excuses for himself and accepted none from others. He has always been relentless in the demands he placed on himself, holding down at one time the posts of President of the Privy Council, Deputy Prime Minister, and Minister of National Defence.
Erik Nielsen for 29 years epitomized the best qualities of parliamentary democracy. He enjoyed friendships on all sides of the House. I appreciated, on behalf of all Members, the generous comments of the Leader of the NDP yesterday, and of the Leader of the Opposition last evening. That was in the finest traditions of Canadian parliamentary life. As I say, Erik enjoyed friendships on all sides of the House, in spite of his reputation as a rough and tumble parliamentary fighter.
Erik has not always been the tough, relentless prosecutor pictured by the media. When circumstances warranted, he has frequently been known to temper the wind to the shorn lambs on the other side. Parliament will miss him, because he is a man who understood Parliament, and who worked tirelessly to make it more effective.
May I express the hope that he can be persuaded to serve Canada in the future in other ways.

subsubtopic: PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday you will recall that I served notice to you of my intention to rise today on a question of privilege. I have now had a chance to review Hansard carefully and I believe my privileges have been breached and that the Standing Orders of this House have been broken. I also served notice of my intention to rise on a question of privilege with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) a few moments ago.
If you deem 1 have a prima facie point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to move the motion necessary to refer the matter to the Parliamentary Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure.
As reported at page 2362 of yesterday's Hansard the Prime Minister said: "If he has had that information for some months why did he not bring it to the attention of the RCMP-" and the next part of the sentence is the truly important part. It states: "-since his failure to do so could result in the obstruction of justice?" By inference, the Prime Minister in the House has accused me of performing a criminal act.
I draw to Your Honour's attention the fact that Section 127 of the Criminal Code very clearly states the definition of "obstructing justice". Clearly, I believe that I have not committed such a criminal act but, beyond that, the Prime Minister does not have the right to make such accusations in

January 20, 1987
Privilege-Mr. Boudria
the House of Commons. I believe, Sir, that if I or anyone else were to accuse another Hon. Member of being a thief, a murderer or any other similar thing, that it would not be permitted by the House, and rightfully so. The same applies to this particular criminal accusation as well.
Section 127 of the Criminal Code deals with judicial proceedings, formal investigations, and attempts to convince others to falsify testimony. While I am not a lawyer, I fail to understand how the Prime Minister could make such accusations since he, of course, is learned in the law.
I draw to Your Honour's attention page 11960 of Hansard of March 19, 1976, where Speaker Jerome stated that where the charge is a direct allegation it must be withdrawn.
Further, I draw to your attention, Sir, Beauchesne's Rules and Forms of the House of Commons of Canada, Fifth Edition, page 107, where it is noted that on several occasions it has been decided that to accuse anyone of an illegal act is improper.
I also draw to Your Honour's attention Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, Fourth Edition, in which the following is stated:
In the Canadian House, questions of privilege take a wide range, but it may be stated in general terms that they refer to all matters affecting the rights and immunities of the house collectively, or to the position and conduct of members in their representative character.
I also draw to Your Honour's attention the following from the same publication which states:
The large number of rulings on the subject of parliamentary language, as applied to a member in debate, clearly indicate that any expression derogatory to his character as an honourable gentleman in private life or to his honour and personal character as a representative of the people is out of order.
On page 362 of the same document it is also pointed out that it is improper to attribute unworthy motives.
Finally, in the same document it states that when a Member has intimated that he would move the adjournment, or that he would in any other way threaten a Member of this House, the Speaker has interposed and called him to order for using language which is menacing to the House. In this case, language which is menacing to a Member is, in my view, menacing to the House of Commons.
In conclusion, I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that Beauchesne's also speaks to this issue. Citation 316 states that to make a personal charge against a Member is against the rules of the House and is identified in certain ways which are set out. Apart from the prohibitions contained in Standing Order 35 it has been sanctioned by usage that a Member, while speaking, must not make a personal charge against a Member.
Citation 326 states that threatening language is also unparliamentary. It states that when a Member has intimated that he would move the adjournment of the House, as I said previously, according to Bourinot, that that indeed would be deemed to be threatening the House and therefore disorderly and improper. For the same reason, and for all the reasons that I have expressed to you today, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the
accusations made yesterday by the Prime Minister are improper and should be withdrawn. If they are not I intend to continue to ask that the matter be referred to the committee responsible for dealing with such matters, if Your Honour finds that I have a prima facie case of privilege.
It is my hope that that will not be necessary and that the Prime Minister will choose to withdraw the unfortunate remarks of yesterday.

It is very clear according to Citation 319 that it is improper "to impute to any Member or Members unworthy motives for
their actions in a particular case". Furthermore, Citation 324 reads:
It is impossible to lay down any specific rules in regard to injurious reflections uttered in debate against particular Members, or to declare beforehand what expressions are or are not contrary to order; much depends upon the tone and manner, and intention, of the person speaking;-
I submit that not only are there grounds for you, Mr. Speaker, to find a prima facie breach of privilege but, in the alternative, to find that the Prime Minister's words were unparliamentary and therefore subject to being declared such by yourself and ordered to be withdrawn.
I also submit that the manner in which the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell approached you yesterday with his concerns about the language used by the Prime Minister, which you were good enough to place on record a few minutes ago, would constitute the notice ordinarily required in order to raise a matter of unparliamentary language.

Member for York South- Weston (Mr. Nunziata) for finding a breach of parliamentary privilege; in any event there are grounds for you to find that the language used by the Prime Minister is unparliamentary and should be withdrawn.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Yesterday during Question Period a question was put by the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) in which he raised the issue as to whether I as Solicitor General did not perform my responsibilities properly and did not act promptly in the matter of allegations against an exempt staff member who worked for the Minister of State. Indeed the Hon. Member's question and request for an RCMP investigation into my role in the affair implies wrongdoing on my part. The facts are as follows, and they will be very brief.
January 20, 1987

On November 5, 1986 my office received correspondence from a Montreal citizen that included allegations against unnamed individuals, including an unnamed staff member in an unnamed cabinet Minister's office.
On November 7, in keeping with standard practice in such cases, my office forwarded the correspondence to the RCMP for review, and a reply was made to the citizen's letter on December 19, 1986, indicating that those concerns were being looked into by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
On November 17, 1986 the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) provided me with copies of that correspondence, asking assurance that I would turn that over to the RCMP. I assured that Hon. Member by letter on November 27, 1986 that indeed I had already done so.
I was advised by the RCMP of the results of this investigation on January 8, 1987, and within hours the member of the ministerial staff was relieved of his duties.
Further, I am advised that the RCMP has no record of being informed with respect to this matter in May 1986, as the Hon. Member for York South-Weston has stated.
The Solicitor General has no responsibility for the administration of the Government's security clearance screening program. I reject categorically the suggestion that I was in any way involved in the security screening process in this case. As the chief law enforcement official for the Government of Canada and as a Member of Parliament, I cannot allow these imputations and allegations to go unchallenged.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: POINTS OF ORDER
speechtext:
I see the Hon. Member for York South- Weston (Mr. Nunziata) indicating that he wishes to rise in response to the point of order of the Hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher). Of course I will hear the Hon. Member, but I want him to know that I have looked over very carefully the comments complained of. It would seem-and this may help shorten debate-that the Hon. Member for York South- Weston asked a question in which he said that it concerned the conduct of two Ministers, one being the Solicitor General. He was asking why a routine security check could not have been done and indicating that the Solicitor General, at least on the information which apparently the Hon. Member had at that time or perhaps thought he had, was notified in October.
Then the question is: in view of this will the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) initiate an RCMP investigation into the conduct of another Member, but this matter concerns the Solicitor General.

Mr. Speaker, I spent the holidays in my riding, in my three riding offices, from December 19 to January 15, being available to the local population and explaining what the softwood lumber issue was all about. As a parliamentarian, I felt a moral responsibility to be in my riding to listen to the people and to explain the repercussions of the 15 per cent tax to the local media. When we take the time to explain the events and the agreement to our people and our industries in Abitibi-Temiscamingue, we find that they have been through worse in the past, Mr. Speaker. For families like the Perrons

and the Bienvenues in Abitibi, who came to the area 50 years ago, working for the forest industry in Abitibi-Temiscamingue was not always easy. These people have been through worse. We had to act and we did so in the best interests of Canadians. People in our regions understand this. They know that the forest industry is subject to fluctuations, that it is a cyclical industry. After the 1983 victory the forest industry increased its softwood lumber exports to the United States. Our share of the American market expanded from 25 to 33 per cent, or thereabouts. Inevitably, sooner or later the Americans were bound to say enough is enough. The American industry put up an impressive and influential lobby which made strong representations to Government authorities and, in the past year, their signals and messages have been clear. Lawyers

representing both countries were quite sure that this time countervailing duties would be imposed. For a year our Canadian ambassador in Washington had been telling the federal Government, the provinces and the forest industry to get ready because the next time around everything would break loose and we would have to negotiate every inch of the way.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to recall briefly the chronology of events during 1986. Mr. Speaker, in late May or early June the alarm was sounded: the American Commerce Department Secretary was considering launching an investigation into the allegedly illegal Canadian softwood lumber competition in the United States and thinking in terms of imposing a 35 to 36 per cent levy on our softwood lumber exports. This was in early June, Mr. Speaker. At the time the Secretary of State for External Affairs vehemently expressed our anger with respect to the American reaction. They were talking about 36 per cent, and this was enough to prompt us to marshall the most elaborate concerted effort of all interested parties in this country, including forest industry spokesmen, federal and provincial Governments, and labour unions. We set up one of the most extensive consultation process ever seen in this country on such an important issue. Mr. Speaker, consultations were held from beginning to end in this case, and nobody will ever be able to claim that the dispute was unilaterally settled by the federal Government. What should be understood, Mr. Speaker, is that natural resources like lumber belong to the provinces. It was the provinces' responsibility to defend their interest, but it was felt the federal Government was in a better position to do so. We decided to get involved because the industry and the provinces called on us to solve the matter on their behalf. This shows we did not act unilaterally but in consultation at all times.
Back to the sequence of events, Mr. Speaker, I was referring to early June, when the U.S. announced or planned a 36 per cent tax, which was unacceptable. I personally rose on two occasions in this House on behalf of the forest industry of Quebec and of my own area, to oppose that 36 per cent tax and to support the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) who had issued a call for calm and action, which we heeded.
So, on June 13, federal and provincial ministers decided to meet-that was on June 13, 1986, Mr. Speaker-to work out a strategy and fight that planned 36 per cent tax on our lumber exports. Again, during the whole summer of 1986, the various parties involved in the issue worked steadily answering a questionnaire, a sort of indictment, at the request of the U.S. Secretary of State. Because of alleged illegal competition, we had to produce a 7,000 page document in answer to the American questionnaire-7,000 pages, Mr. Speaker. We would be faced with exactly the same kind of thing if we had decided to go through the legal process-the Americans would have won the day and we would have been forced at any time-the industry, the governments, the various levels of Government-to open our books and to fill 7,000 page
questionnaires as we had to submit on August 13. There would have been several of them in the future, and the industry was not interested in getting stuck in that red tape any longer.
Mr. Speaker, on September 13, 1986, the Government reached the practical decision to work out a strategy to offer a compromise to the industry and to our American friends. We brought forth, we proposed to the Americans a 10 per cent compromise. That was no unilateral step by the Government. The forest industry and the provinces were in agreement. We felt that, faced with a 36 per cent evil, why not come up ourselves with a less stringent proposal, let us say 10 per cent. We submitted that proposal on September 30 in a diplomatic note that went to the Embassy, to the U.S. Government in Washington, and the answer was no. That proposal was turned down, and later there was a preliminary finding that was not in our favour and there also was a 15 per cent proposal submitted by the American Government. So we met at a federal-provincial conference on November 20-21, one month before the December 30 deadline that had been set for the 15 per cent proposal.
Mr. Speaker, during the two-day federal-provincial conference held on November 20 and 21, we had to act and find a solution to a problem that had to be solved. There were three alternatives: first, go through the legal process, all the way- that was the Ontario position, the one that was often advocated here by their Big Brother in this House. However, Mr. Speaker, it is clear that this legal process was prejudicial to Canada. It would probably have meant the implementation of a tax exceeding 15 per cent and such a tax might not have been collected by the federal treasury and would probably have been set at 30, 35 or 25 per cent, a level which would have been most detrimental.
The second possible alternative would have been to withdraw from the negotiations as I have heard it suggested, Mr. Speaker, but that was not a solution. The United States would have carried on and would probably have levied, as I said earlier, a 30 p. 100 tax which would have entailed a terrible loss of jobs in Canada.
The third alternative was that as reasonable people, and as responsible governments which would like to solve the problem, we would find a third solution and reach a compromise. This is why we should congratulate our Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) and our Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) who sought the agreement of nine provinces. However, it should be stated, Mr. Speaker, that following extensive consultations, nine provinces out of ten approved the arrangement put forward at the federal-provincial conference. We should reconsider that arrangement which clearly stated that the 15 per cent tax appeared to us as the lesser evil, but the main thing was that the revenues were reinvested in Canada and redistributed among the provinces and it is on that issue that we won the day. This is not a major victory about which we should be mightily pleased. No, but as the elected government we had to
