that Bill C-229, an Act to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act, the Canada Labour Code and the Public Service Employment Act (whistleblowing), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-229 is an Act to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act, the Canada Labour Code and the Public Service Employment Act. This could be referred to as the whistleblowing Act.
The purpose of this Bill is to provide appropriate sanctions against retaliatory discharges by public sector employers of employees who report or blow the whistle on serious misconduct of their employers.
In protecting employees acting in good faith, this Bill would recognize that there are times when it is in the public's interest to encourage employee whistleblowing, particularly when the public health and safety are at issue. The price of doing right should not be the end of a career, scorn, or years of economic hardship.
This legislation is intended to protect people who are willing to expose illegal or unethical practices of their employers. It would allow employees to file with the Canadian Human Rights Commission information concerning actions of their employers which they believe to be a threat to the health and safety of the general public.
The Canadian Human Rights Commission would then determine if the revelations of the employee were made in good faith. If the Canadian Human Rights Commission decided that there was no malicious intent on the part of the employee, that individual would have the benefit of all protective measures provided by this legislation. Specifically, protection would be provided from dismissal, suspension, or the imposition of a financial penalty by an employer in retaliation for a complaint, or for a disclosure in connection with a complaint.
If the Canadian Human Rights Commission is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the allegations contained in a complaint are true, and that it is in the public interest to reveal the allegations, the Commission would file an appropriate report to the Speaker of the House of Commons. Every report submitted to the House of Commons would be referred to a designated committee for the purpose of reviewing the ethics of conduct of public officials.
By providing appropriate protection for employees acting in good faith, this Bill recognizes that there are instances when it is in the best interests of the public to encourage employee whistleblowing. When the health and safety of the public are in jeopardy, this Bill will provide a clear and much superior method than the usual brown envelope procedure. This topic has not received as much attention in Canada as it has in the United States. I believe it is time for this type of legislation in Canada.
Whistleblowers have been called many names such as rats, traitors, publicity seekers, alarmists, trouble-makers, malcontents, weasels, and stool pigeons, to name a few. To some they have been branded as moral heroes. Recent studies in the United States suggest that whistleblowers are ordinary employees who are so troubled by the employers' conduct that they feel compelled to do something. Frequently, employers respond to such action by terminating their employment.
I believe that individuals who blow the whistle for legitimate reasons such as gross mismanagement, waste of public funds, fraud, corruption, as well as the health and safety of the general public, should, if proof can be established, be encouraged to protect society, and in turn have protection themselves. However, this Bill deals with the health and safety aspect of whistleblowing, and I feel it would be an important step. We should protect those who show courage, ethics,
January 20, 1987

conscience, or moral concerns instead of blindly following orders from superiors, or looking the other way. The important thing to remember is not just the protection of a legitimate whistleblower, but the general public who may well be in danger.
It is time that we, as legislators, looked at what happens to whistleblowers after the events that could well change their lives. Whistleblowers almost inevitably pay a heavy price. With few exceptions, they are driven out of not just their jobs but their professions. It is long overdue that we give consideration to protecting those people who have legitimate public health and safety concerns, and have first-hand knowledge that the information is being suppressed.
Despite the need for this whistleblower's protection and the public concern for it, industry and Government remain cool to the idea. It would be a small price to pay for this legislation to protect society, and the careers and the emotional lives of conscientious whistleblowers.
For example, ethical whistleblowers exposing PCB dangers, harmful plant operations, environmental pollution, questionable food additives, violations of safety regulations, should be protected as they have a responsibility to our society. It has been established that most whistleblowers are loyal employees with many years of faithful service. They are not habitual complainers, members of the lunatic fringe, or anarchists bent on violent change. They are people who come face to face with a practice that they believe is wrong and decide to turn concern into action.
Only after first taking their concerns to the appropriate management, and then without action, would they have to use this Bill as protection. Instead of receiving thanks for bringing their legitimate concerns to light, they could presently be charged with damaging morale, hindering efficiency, or performing their duties incompetently. With this legislation, they would be protected. Even the union, if one existed, or if the employee was a member, might be reluctant to take up the issue.
The individual, or perhaps several people, would have the other options I stated earlier: the brown envelope method, the use of the media, or to seek assistance from their Member of Parliament to expose the wrongdoing. Normally, employees have a duty to respect the confidentiality of information learned through their employment which could be damaging to their employer. However, this does not apply to knowledge about actual known or planned crime. Thus the need for this legislation.
Whistleblowing is serious. This Bill intends to encourage the truth in order to protect the health and safety of Canadians through a legitimate process which would also protect the whistleblower. I ask that the House of Commons seriously consider this Bill by referring it to the appropriate committee for study.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADIAN HUMAN RIGHTS ACT, CANADA LABOUR CODE, PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I wish to congratulate the Hon. Member for Hastings-Frontenac- Lennox and Addington (Mr. Vankoughnet) for introducing
Canadian Human Rights Act
what I think is a very valuable and very needed piece of legislation. I agree with the Bill. I would support sending the Bill to a committee for further study and consideration, and possibly amendments which we are all open to. I wish to tell him in speaking to some public servants in my riding who over the years have come to me with this difficult problem of whistleblowing on their employer for reasons of health and safety that in their opinion, this is a much needed and important piece of legislation.
I repeat, I congratulate the Hon. Member on his initiative, and I hope the House sees fit to pass this legislative suggestion in due course.

Mr. Speaker, the Bill before the House today deals with a question that sometimes creates problems for Government employees. As far as I know, there is no appropriate sanction in Canada to deal with retaliatory discharges by public sector employers of employees who report or "blow the whistle" on serious misconduct of their employers, particularly, as the Bill says, with respect to health and safety. By thus protecting employees against retaliatory action on the part of an employer who is unhappy about the fact that an employee has revealed certain information, I think we are recognizing the fact that the public interest sometimes requires that employees working in the public sector and who feel obliged to take action on matters or situations they find unacceptable, have the right to see and consult with a public person or an ombudsman and to tell that person, if they so wish, that they do not agree with a given measure because it constitutes a threat to public health and safety.

This whole question came to light some time ago, but Hon. Members will recall that articles appeared in the newspapers in 1986 dealing with an employee who had been fired from the Immigration Appeal Board.
I refer to an article by Philip Jalsevac which appeared in the February 13, 1986 edition of the Kitchener-Waterloo Record and read:
The Immigration Appeal Board has followed the five-month suspension of a Toronto deputy registrar by firing him for giving internal documents to a lawyer and publicly criticizing the board.
It went on to explain what board chairman Michel Falar-deau-Ramsay told Registrar Keith Forgie, 35, in the letter of dismissal which he received the previous day.
The Canada Employment and Immigration Union, through its spokesperson, Renaud Paquet, said that it would pursue the matter. At the time I was asked to comment, and I said that I believed legislation should be forthcoming. I also said that I believed strongly that a White Paper should be brought forward by the then Minister of Justice, espousing the Government's views on the matter. We asked for a discussion paper or a draft Bill from the Government. Our only reply was from the Minister of Justice who indicated the Government's position.

January 20, 1987
Canadian Human Rights Act
I should like to quote from another article written by Philip Jalsevac which read:
Justice Minister John Crosbie says he can't see the need for legislation to protect public servants who make public improper or illegal government practices.
The article continued:
However, he said his immediate reaction was that so-called whistleblowing laws aren't needed because public servants are protected like everybody else by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
I think that point is well taken. We in the House know that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms is before the courts for interpretation, but that is not the point.
There are other jurisdictions in the world, such as American jurisdictions, where certain protection is afforded people who for reasons of security, possibly safety, or health feel that a procedure or something they are being asked to do is against the national interest.

Mr. Speaker, the concept of whistleblowing or whistleblowers is to be seen as an attempt to resolve the dilemma of employee loyalty and an employer responsible for running a public agency.
As I said earlier, in this context Canada provides no general protection for whistleblowers against retaliatory measures on the part of the employer. Federal public servants in particular have no legal protection should they reveal information on hazards to public safety.
The only legal protection at the federal level concerns the application of specific legislation. For instance, the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Canada Labour Code contain provisions that protect individuals against possible retaliatory action by the employer if they file complaints, testify or in any way participate in the enforcement of that specific legislation as it applies to their employer. This legal protection does not cover whistleblowing on activities that put the community at risk.
However, although not specifically aimed at whistleblowing cases, certain statutes may be referred to in support of whistleblowers. For instance, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) pointed out, Section 2 of the Canadian Charter of Rights provides protection for fundamental freedoms like freedom of opinion, expression and conscience. The mere reference to these freedoms does not protect whistleblowers, but since the courts are now in the process of interpreting the Charter, it might be a useful reference. As we know, everything depends on the court interpretation of the facts in the spirit of the Charter, Mr. Speaker. It is there, but it needs to be enhanced and interpreted by the courts.
On the other hand, the Access to Information Act might be useful to protect whistleblowers. As a matter of fact, if any disclosed information could have been obtained through this statute, it would mitigate the notion that a public servant must
respect confidentiality with respect to his employer. Recourse to the provisions of this act does not by itself guarantee the protection of whistleblowers, but it can change the picture to the extent that the whistleblowing incident itself would become less dramatic.
Finally, given the absence of a legislative provision, common law might be used as a guideline. There have been a few such cases in American common law, and the result was that the protection given to whisleblowers is related to the accuracy and veracity of the information disclosed, as well as to the existence of real danger for the community. The burden of proof therefore weighs very heavily on the whistleblower. However, legal precedents have failed to establish criteria to enable us to assess the extent of evidence to be submitted with respect to real danger, nor have they given us a precise definition of the notion of community.
Therefore whistleblowers in Canada do not enjoy general protection and they can resort only indirectly to their means of defence against the possibility of retaliatory measures taken by their employer. A whistleblower acts at his own risk.
As I said earlier, the situation is different in the United States because they do have specific provisions barring any retaliatory measure against an employee who has disclosed information pertaining to any kind of danger for the public.
Mr. Speaker, I know that I have only two minutes left, which is not much. I wish to recommend most seriously to the House that it refer the subject matter of this well drafted and well considered bill to a committee for study and review and that it ask the Government for its support, because it is important that civil servants moved by their concern for public health and safety be protected against retaliatory measures when they make public statements about measures they are supposed to take on behalf of their employer.
Mr. Speaker, I should like again to congratulate the Hon. Member for introducing this bill and indicate to him that we support it. I hope that this bill is read a second time today.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADIAN HUMAN RIGHTS ACT, CANADA LABOUR CODE, PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter into this debate partly because of my concerns about the rights of federal public servants, a number of whom I have in my constituency. However, I think it is a broader issue, as the Hon. Member for	Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and
Addington (Mr. Vankoughnet) would of course maintain.
We suffer from the constitutional dilemma that the area of federal jurisdiction in Canada over employee-employer relations is considerably more limited relative to the total number of people in the workforce than perhaps it is in the United States where whistleblowing legislation has become quite common both at the federal level and at the level of state Governments.
January 20, 1987

The fact that the jurisdiction is more limited should not, I believe, prevent this Government and this level of Government from acting on behalf of those employees that are within its jurisdiction, and 1 hope in that case setting an example which will be followed by a number of provincial Governments in short order if Ottawa were to take the lead. I agree with the Hon. Member's proposal that Bill C-229 should be sent to a legislative committee and considered very carefully. I endorse the principles of the Bill. I think the idea of whistleblower legislation would benefit particularly larger organizations under federal jurisdiction. First and foremost would be the Government of Canada as well as the large Crown corporations.
I say to my friend on the benches opposite that I fear the Bill is rather weak and needs to be reworked substantially, but it would be better to do that in committee than to deny a committee the chance because I do not think the issues are that difficult to resolve. There are ample precedents that can be followed, and it would be my hope that a committee with a month or two of work and perhaps with some submissions and interventions from people knowledgeable about these matters could come back with a Bill that would serve us well.
This is a good idea but the mechanics are somewhat questionable. Just what is it we are looking for and what can be done in order to ensure that the whistleblower is respected? We have to deal with people who say; "You are going to create anarchy in the workplace" or those who say, "you are going to create a Bill which offers too little encouragement or offers too little protection to someone who feels that they should raise problems of health and safety, violation of public property, public policy or of gross mismanagement". People feel compelled to raise the issue in some way. How do you arrive at a balance on those questions?
There are really two issues. One is to provide what I would call a conventional means by which whistleblowers can lodge their complaints. It remains open to somebody who is very concerned about a particular issue and who just wants to blow on the issue to call a press conference or bring a banner to Parliament Hill or in some other way complain. The passage of whistleblower legislation will not do away with that remedy which is available right now.
The problem, of course, is that most people who blow the whistle in that way, except in exceptional circumstances, have to realize that they are taking their own fate in hand, that they carry a grave risk that they may get dismissed for disloyalty or for behaviour which is unacceptable to the employer. As well, many employers would be prepared to fire the employee for that kind of behaviour even if it cost them some money in severance pay to do so. That is why the whistleblower legislation which has been adopted in a number of American jurisdictions has tended to provide some means by which complaints can be lodged on a basis of confidence but which can be investigated without identifying the source of the complaint, by which the complainant can find out what was
Canadian Human Rights Act
done, what was determined with respect to his complaint and what action, if any, was taken.
In certain cases there is still an ultimate step which leads to publicity of the complaint but, even in that case, it is often the agency or the investigating body which carries the complaint rather than leaving the individual employee in a situation where he or she risks an intolerable situation in the workplace by being identified as the whistleblower in public to his or her supervisors and employer.
The second part of the legislation is to protect the complainant. Confidentiality is a major means of protecting the complainant, but the American legislation also generally provides for anti-discrimination provisions which also have the effect of protecting the complainant against what the U.S. Federal Code calls personnel action, a generic term which includes not only dismissal but also being passed over on promotions, getting bad evaluations on performance reviews every six months or other types of actions that may have a direct or indirect impact on a person's employment prospects or on his or her ability to do the job effectively.
The Bill proposed by the Hon. Member for Hastings- Frontenac-Lennox and Addington does provide a mechanism through the Human Rights Commission to protect complainants against that kind of personnel action. I think my major concern is the fact that the avenue for complaints is not spelled out at all effectively, in fact I do not believe it is spelled out adequately. I think the Bill might benefit in committee. If it does not get to committee because it is talked out-I would hope that does not occur-then I hope the Hon. Member would be encouraged by the reaction in this House and perhaps go back to the drawing board and elaborate on that part of the Bill to come up with something that might be a more effective or workable model which, as I said, I can agree to and do agree to in principle.
I would cite the U.S. Federal Code, Mr. Speaker, which applies to members of the American federal Public Service and also, I presume, to a number of federal boards, agencies and commissions. The same principle about protecting the whistleblower exists. The same principle about providing protection against job action exists as has been provided for in rather briefer form in this Bill. What also occurs is that in separate legislation the Congress has adopted what it calls an inspector general system.
There are inspector general offices in all of the major American departments of Government. As Hon. Members know, the American ministries or departments are much larger than ours. They have only 10 members of Cabinet so those 10 departments make up what most of us cover off with 30 or 40 ministries in Canada. In addition, there are certain administrations such as the space agency, the veterans administration and small business administration which also have inspectors general.
Those inspectors general have a mandate to combat fraud, abuse and mismanagement. They do that not only at their own

January 20, 1987
Canadian Human Rights Act
initiative but can also receive and act on complaints. The inspector general stands in relation to the department to which he or she is appointed. I presume they have some kind of a small office of investigators in much the same way as say our Auditor General stands in relation to the Government of Canada, that is, an independent relationship. Therefore, complaints from whistleblowers, from people who wish to raise matters with the inspector general can be raised. Matters of health and safety, abuse, fraud or mismanagement can all be raised. There is a means by which the employee is entitled to find out what happened to a particular complaint.
I do not know if that legislation is perfect. A very useful paper was distributed and prepared by Mr. David Johansen of the law and government division of our own Library of Parliament. In the literature there is some question in the United States as to what extent legislation should actively encourage whistleblowers and to what extent it should simply recognize that people wish and have an urge to blow the whistle. It should at least allow that to take place without people putting their jobs in jeopardy when they lodge complaints.
Also cited in the same paper is some very useful legislation in the State of Connecticut. I might read one or two clauses into the record. In Connecticut the statutory provision states:
Any state employee-having knowledge of any matter involving corruption, unethical practices, violation of state laws or regulations, mismanagement, gross waste of funds, abuse of authority or danger to the public safety occurring in any state department or agency may transmit all facts and information in his possession concerning such matter to the attorney general-
The attorney general is the designated hitter in this case:
-who shall make such investigation as he thinks proper. The attorney general shall have power to summon witnesses, require the production of any necessary books, papers or other documents and administer oaths to witnesses, where necessary, for the purpose of investigation.
It might be useful to have that kind of process even with respect to such things as the events that are now taking place or that have taken place in St. Jean-Sur-Richelieu. The clause continues:
Upon the conclusion of his investigation, the attorney general shall (a) where necessary, report his findings to the governor, or in matters involving criminal activity, to the chief state's attorney, and (2) report to the complainant, upon his request, on such findings and any actions pursuant thereto. The attorney general shall not, after receipt of any information from a state employee under the provisions of this section-disclose the identity of such employee without his consent unless he determines that such disclosure is unavoidable during the course of his investigation.
There is a limit on personal action and as well a limitation that provides that if an employee is found to have knowingly lodged false charges, the employee puts himself or herself at some risk.
I think there are some valuable precedents in the United States. I realize my time is up but I would ask Hon. Members to look sympathetically at this proposal. While I do believe that the principle should be sustained, possibly the provision
might be worked up in more detail so that we could have more effective whistleblower legislation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Chuck Cook (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADIAN HUMAN RIGHTS ACT, CANADA LABOUR CODE, PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to address the Bill to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act to protect so-called whistleblowers, by which I understand the Hon. Member to mean public servants who speak out to the news media or to Members of this House on alleged instances of government wrongdoing or misinformation. The concept of the Bill, as I understand it, is that unless those in positions of authority are subject to possible serious sanctions and punishment, they will seek to retaliate in the form of harassment and persecution of the employee or employees concerned.
Let me first say that I find this a concept which reflects a certain lack of awareness of the fine system of Public Service employee protection measures which have been built up in Canada over the last 120 years and which already permit employees to bring their concerns to the attention of Departmental management. I feel rather strongly that in this day and age, internal systems are in place that minimize or eliminate any need for so-called whistleblowing by employees.
The overwhelming majority of employees and appointed officials in the Public Service are hard-working, trustworthy and honest people who would take appropriate action using existing channels when instances of wrongdoing are uncovered by them or are brought to their attention. I believe there are adequate systems in place to ensure that any employee has access through internal routes to appropriate authorities. However, in extreme circumstances where employees might find themselves frustrated in attempts to get their messages through to officials of sufficient seniority, a whistleblowing situation might-and, I repeat, might-be envisaged. It is to this unlikely scenario that I would now turn.
I believe that the picture painted by this Bill is one of a Public Service in which employees are devoid of rights, of protection from harassment and persecution and of all redress mechanisms to guarantee their fair treatment and are generally subject to such a regimen that only amended human rights legislation could bring their mistreatment into the open and thereby control those who mistreat them. This image of the Public Service is, in my belief, at odds with reality. I believe Hon. Members would share that belief. Any image less reflective of today's reality in the Public Service is hard to imagine.
I make no claim to be an expert on Public Service redress methods, but I have investigated some of them. All Hon. Members are surely aware of the impressive body of existing personnel legislation and the rights these laws have afforded public servants over the years. Let us take a look at these laws.
Pursuing scenarios, let us suppose that after an alleged whistleblowing incident, a manager were to decide to punish the whistleblower. Could he or she do so with impunity? The answer is clearly no. Let us suppose a boss seeks to punish an employee by means of an annual performance appraisal that

January 20, 1987

unfairly denigrates the employee's abilities. Such an action is immediately subject to the full rigours of the grievance procedures accorded to public servants by the wishes of this House under the Public Service Staff Relations Act (1967). I would remind the House of the comprehensive nature of this grievance process. Following a complaint, an aggrieved employee may have up to four further levels of hearings of his or her case before Departmental officers of increasing seniority until the case receives the personal attention of the Deputy Minister of the Department. In addition, in many cases employees would have the active support of their unions or associations in this regard.
Let us suppose again that based on some alleged whistleblowing incident, the manager attempts to build a case for the release of the employee based on grounds of incompetence or incapacity. First, such an action is always based on performance appraisal reports which are subject to the redress mechanisms I have already indicated. Second, a decision to release an employee under this provision which is contained in Section 31 of the Public Service Employment Act is appealable. The first level of appeal is to the Public Service Commission's Appeals and Investigations Branch, a quasi-judicial tribunal. Should satisfaction not be found there, the aggrieved party may have recourse to the Federal Court and may eventually appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada itself.
In this regard, Hon. Members are no doubt aware that cases involving release or discharge under the Public Service's personnel legislation have indeed found their way to the Supreme Court. These actions have served to clarify the boundaries of legitimate managerial prerogative and conduct. Several of these cases have caused the learned judges of the Supreme Court to speak eloquently of the democratic rights of public servants in Canada. The very fact that these cases reach and are heard in detail by the Supreme Court is a tribute to the breadth and equity of the redress systems already available to public servants.
Next, let us suppose that the punishment selected by this imaginary but vindictive manager is to try to damage forever the employee's prospects of career advancement. Can this actually be done? No, it cannot be done because for every job opening that comes up in those parts of the Public Service where the employee is eligible to be considered, a potential appeal action may be brought to the Public Service Commission if he or she is not considered. From the appeals directorate, it goes up through that same network of redress through the courts I have already cited.
Frustrated on these points, this manager is in a little trouble about now. Let us say that the manager now seeks to punish the employee via the disciplinary route. All disciplinary action against employees stems from the powers granted to the employer to establish and maintain standards of conduct and discipline under the Financial Administration Act while the redress for employees is contained in the Public Service Staff Relations Act. Again, detailed and exhaustive multi-level
Canadian Human Rights Act
grievance mechanisms already exist to protect employees from arbitrary and unfair action.
In addition to the internal grievance procedures I have already outlined, in these circumstances still further redress rights apply. Should satisfaction still not have been received in the view of the grievor at the final level of internal Departmental grievance review, further action is available through the Public Service Staff Relations Board which will appoint an adjudicator to investigate the matter. Even after that hearing, which may now be the fifth hearing of the case, redress lies through the courts. These are comprehensive rights indeed. Rights such as these would almost be unheard of in the private sector.
By this stage, our manager has run out of avenues to pursue in causing the employee's release by building a dossier of negative performance appraisals, by building a case for release on the grounds of incompetence or incapacity, by attempting to frustrate the employee's career path or by seeking a discharge on disciplinary grounds. All that is left is for the manager to attempt to make the employee's life miserable. However, such a campaign constitutes personal harassment and personal harassment is a most serious offence in the Public Service. If such action is wrongly taken, it constitutes a prima facie case of abuse of authority.
In addition to the normal grievance route, the employee may elect to pursue redress through the personal harassment policy. The first step is to see the Departmental personal harassment co-ordinator. This individual is responsible for the investigation of all alleged cases of personal harassment within a given Department. If the co-ordinator cannot rectify the issue, he can take the case to the investigation director and so on. In other words, this Act is really unnecessary given the splendid Public Service and various methods of redress we have.
I trust I have illustrated, at least in general terms, the breadth of rights, entitlements, recourses and redress mechanisms, both formal and informal, already enjoyed in the Public Service of Canada. I trust the House will realize this protection is strong enough to protect anyone seeking to address concerns of genuine wrongdoing and to thereby protect the public interest.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Paliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State and Minister responsible for Multiculturalism):

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADIAN HUMAN RIGHTS ACT, CANADA LABOUR CODE, PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to deal with Bill C-229 introduced by my hon. colleague. I do not share the views expressed by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Centre (Mr. Cassidy) and the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). Indeed, I do not even agree with the principle involved.
First of all, I wish to say that private employers have always expected loyalty and productivity from their employees. In the public sector, the Government here in Ottawa must respect its

January 20, 1987
Canadian Human Rights Act
employees and cannot insist on productivity. It insists on loyalty and confidentiality. These are the only two things which I expect from my employees, because when they accepted their positions, they agreed on loyalty and confidentiality. The Canadian public already has a right to access to information. With Bill C-229, the Hon. Member would like to go even further and ask the Government to surrender confidentiality. As the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) said earlier, we agree with the principle, but this Bill certainly needs improvements.
Of course, people need information, but I suggest that they have been overwhelmed with confidential data over the past two and a half years. We get them in newspapers every day. Many in my riding feel that the Opposition is doing a tremendous job. It finds, sees and denounces everything. They are wrong, for it is not the Opposition which is doing a good job, but the journalists who obtain information through informers, the so-called "whistleblowers". As I said to my constituents, the Opposition makes no investigation and discovers nothing, being satisfied with buying the morning paper and reading the news. After meeting for one hour, it is ready to ask the Government embarrassing questions during the oral question period on everything that happens. If the news is somewhat positive, it will make it negative. And who are these people who inform the newspapermen? Well, they are the famous "whistleblowers". I like this phrase very much.
So to achieve this, Mr. Speaker, this Bill would have to amend the Canadian Labour Code, the Canadian Human Rights Act, and the Public Service Employment Act. The Canadian Human Rights Act would be amended so that discharging or suspending an employee, imposing a monetary sanction or putting him at a disadvantage would constitute a discriminatory act which the Canadian Human Rights Commission would be empowered to examine and correct. For instance, if an employee had good reasons to believe that his employer was acting illegally or against the public interest or was endangering public health or safety, he could lay a complaint before the Canadian Human Rights Commission, which would have the power to provide some protection in relation with disclosures made in good faith, going as far as rolling back retaliatory measures taken by the employer.
In this context, any disciplinary action by the employer against an employee could be viewed as an infraction.
If the complaint is founded, the Commission would refer any misconduct of a public sector employer to the House of Commons and its "Ethics Committee". As for the Canada Labour Code, it would be amended to specify that retaliatory discharges for bona fide whistleblowing will be considered as unwarranted or unjust.
In addition, an employee would not necessarily be guilty of disloyalty for making disclosures about his employer. Protection of denunciators is not a new idea, Mr. Speaker, and in this era of commitment to open Government, a number of countries have passed legislation for this purpose. However, attempts to legislate in this vast and important intermediary
zone where an individual is neither obligated to respect a law nor free to act as he wishes have not always had the expected results.
The 1978 American Public Service Reform Act of which the two previous speakers have spoken protects public servants who make certain revelations against retaliation. It prohibits the imposition of sanctions by the officers in charge to the employee who has disclosed certain information. However the law is formulated and whatever the protection it gives denunciators, there will always remain a difficult question. What are the motives of the denunciators? This is where it becomes interesting, Mr. Speaker. Denunciation can be a defensive mechanism on the part of an employee under threat of disciplinary or other type of action for reasons which have no relation with the apparent misconduct. In other words, a public servant about to be discharged for unsatisfactory work might want to protect himself by accusing his superiors of misconduct. This could also be a catharsis for personal and organizational conflicts unrelated with the apparent misconduct. But in other terms, Mr. Speaker, all this could become some kind of a blackmail.
Could you tell me, for instance, Mr. Speaker, what good faith means? We all think we act in good faith, and believe me since I came here in Ottawa, I have often wondered about the definition of good faith. We all believe we act in good faith, and would never admit we could act otherwise. So, how could we then define good faith or the lack of it? How does the Bill succeed in enlightening us on that matter? It does not seem easy to me to define with enough clarity the concept of good faith.
I have another comment to make about this Bill. It seeks to protect employees blowing the whistle on an employer who is planning to act contrary to public policy. What is contrary to such policy? Some will say that any major change in public policy is contrary to that public policy until the Government has decided to amend it. There can be confusion between what is perceived as contrary to public policy and what is a normal process of change in that policy.
Further, Mr. Speaker, one of the basic principles underlying the public sector is that of employee allegiance and loyalty to their superiors. How are we to reconcile that principle with a Bill that involves a third party, the Canadian Human Rights Commission, in the process, before allowing the time needed for persons who have committed an action that may seem contrary to national interests to justify such action?
Finally, to what extent is the legislation actually needed, if there is nothing to lead us to believe that public sector employers act in a way that violates health and safety?
At present, there are a number of statutes and regulations that deal with industrial relations in the public sector.
For instance, the Canadian Human Rights Act, the very open-minded Access to Information Act, the Canadian Labour Code, the Public Service Staff Relations Act, the Public Service Employment Act and the Staff Harassment Policy do

January 20, 1987

protect public service employees. Consequently, an act to protect them from sanctions by employers for whistleblowing in good faith would even be superfluous.
Let me ask you a question, Mr. Speaker, without even your having to answer. Who would hire a "whistleblower"? Who would hire someone who was not loyal or who could not keep his or her employer's confidentiality, for instance? That would be a conventional employee violation, but the employee who would do that kind of thing might have to live with those problems all his or her life, and this is where I say that at some point the grievance process could be used, but grievances only afford protection against harassment, discrimination and so on, but there is no way a grievance could protect against a lack of loyalty or confidentiality.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADIAN HUMAN RIGHTS ACT, CANADA LABOUR CODE, PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the motivation of the Hon. Member for Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Van-koughnet) for bringing this Bill forward, but I cannot help but believe that the Canadian Human Rights Act is not the appropriate place for the proposed provisions. To understand why I feel this way, it is useful to know some of the background to the development of the Canadian Human Rights Act and, indeed, other human rights legislation in the country.
Following the Second World War Canadians and members of other democratic nations became sensitive to the need to have effective mechanisms for protecting minorities against prejudice and discrimination. In 1948 the United Nations proclaimed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights which affirmed "the dignity and worth of the human person" and that "all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights". The Universal Declaration also asserts that: "All are entitled to equal protection against any discrimination in violation of this declaration."
It was in this spirit that our early human rights laws were developed. Initially, these laws were quasi-criminal in nature and were enforced by officials of government Departments. These laws eventually evolved into our contemporary human rights statutes which take a more remedial approach. These statutes are designed to encourage the conciliation and settlement of complaints, and are administered generally by agencies and commissions which operate independently of the Government.
The Canadian Human Rights Act is administered by the Canadian Human Rights Commission. The Commission investigates complaints of discrimination and may appoint a conciliator to attempt to settle a complaint. If the complaint is not settled and the Commission believes that the complaint should not be dismissed, the Commission may request the President of the Human Rights Tribunal panel to appoint a tribunal to hear the complaint. The tribunal, which is an independent and impartial body, adjudicates the complaint
Canadian Human Rights Act
and may order appropriate remedies if it finds that discrimination has occurred. This model of enforcement is followed by several jurisdictions in Canada.
The point of these laws has always been to combat discrimination and to ensure that all individuals have an equal opportunity to participate in Canadian society. It is worth quoting the purpose clause of the Canadian Human Rights Act which is as follows:
The purpose of this Act is to extend the present laws in Canada to give effect-to the principle that every individual should have an equal opportunity with other individuals to make for himself or herself the life that he or she is able and wishes to have, consistent with his or her duties and obligations as a member of society, without being hindered in or prevented from doing so by discriminatory practices based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex, marital status, family status, disability or conviction for an offence for which a pardon has been granted.
The principle of equal opportunity is a principle to which the Government is fully committed. The Canadian Human Rights Act is one of the vehicles through which this commitment is realized. Hon. Members will understand, then, my reluctance to support amendments to this Act which would not fit together with its essential thrust.
The Canadian Human Rights Act currently provides protection on the basis of a number of prohibited grounds of discrimination including race, sex, colour, religion, national or ethnic origin, or disability. These grounds generally relate to characteristics which are either immutable or difficult to change. The Human Rights Act is designed to assist persons who have been denied an emloyment opportunity or access to services or accommodation because of invidious discrimination. It seems to me, however, that Bill C-229 relates to different concerns outside the principles of the Canadian Human Rights Act.
Bill C-229 would amend the Human Rights Act to provide protection for employees who report the misconduct of their employers, what some people call "whistleblowing". Bill C-229 would call discrimination the discharge or discipline of a "whistleblower". With respect, this is simply not the type of conduct which we have come to describe as discrimination. As far as I know, it is not the type of conduct that is dealt with by any anti-discrimination statutes in Canada. As such, it is not clear to me that such provisions should be grafted or tacked on to the Canadian Human Rights Act. To do so might well dilute the force of the anti-discrimination provisions of the Act as well as the ability of the Canadian Human Rights Commission to deal effectively with racial and other forms of discrimination.
I should point out that while I oppose these amendments to the Canadian Human Rights Act, I welcome efforts to keep the Act up to date in order to do what it is supposed to do, which is to prevent invidious discrimination. I am, therefore, pleased that the Government has committed itself to review the Canadian Human Rights Act in Toward Equality, the Government's response to Equality for All, the report of the Parliamentary Committee on Equality Rights. In Toward Equality the Government also agreed in principle to repeal

those provisions of the Human Rights Act which permit mandatory retirement on a blanket basis. Generally, this will mean that employees cannot be compulsorily retired simply because they have reached what is called "normal age of retirement".
I applaud this commitment because it says that we will no longer abide the stereotypes of our older citizens and of what they can and cannot do. It recognizes that there is a real and continuing contribution which they can make to the economic life of our country. At the same time, I am pleased that the Government is considering transitional rules to ensure the orderly abolition of mandatory retirement. This is a complex area involving many collective agreements and pension plans, and transitional rules may be necessary to prevent undue hardship.
Another amendment to the Canadian Human Rights Act which the Government announced in Toward Equality, and which I support, is to incorporate the concept of reasonable accommodation. The Parliamentary Subcommittee on Equality Rights recommended that the Canadian Human Rights Act require employers to make reasonable accommodation to the special needs of members of classes protected from discrimination, except where this would cause undue hardship to the employer.
This amendment is particularly important to disabled persons to help them overcome the arbitrary barriers to employment. This amendment will also be helpful in providing for the accommodation of the religious observances of employees. It will do so in a reasonable way that balances the needs of employees and the capacity of employers.
These are the sorts of matters with which an anti-discriminatory statute should concern itself. I realize that the title "Canadian Human Rights Act" may have broad connotations, but the Act, like similarly titled provincial legislation, is geared to dealing with discrimination. It concerns specific enforcement mechanisms for dealing with specific types of problems and does not necessarily lend itself to dealing with other sorts of problems, particularly those that are addressed by the Bill which we have before us. I appreciate the intentions of the Hon. Member for Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington and I believe that he may find a different approach more appropriate.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak to Bill C-37, the export charge on softwood lumber. It is of immense importance not only to my constituents but to the country at large.
There is a dreadful tale behind the creation of Bill C-37. The Government has made a number of flip-flops on the whole issue. Last June, when the United States International Trade Commission accepted a petition from the United States softwood lumber producers, there was a clear indication by the Government that it would oppose a countervail duty at that time, which was proposed to be some 27 per cent or 28 per cent. Throughout the summer, all provincial Governments and Departments of Natural Resources spent hundreds of thousands of dollars preparing the necessary documentation. It is my understanding that some 7,000 items were prepared by the various provincial government Departments.
There was unanimity among the forest products industry, the Canadian Forest Industries Council, provincial Governments and the federal Government that the petition before the U.S. Department of Commerce trade administration section would be opposed. In fact, the Minister said that they would oppose it all the way.
Suddenly in late September the Government made a final offer of 10 per cent to the U.S. softwood lumber pricing coalition. We waited until mid-October when that Government came down with a preliminary determination of a countervail of 15 per cent. The Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) indicated that she and the Government would fight this all the way. That decision was supported by the Canadian Forest Industries Council. Suddenly in December, before the First Ministers met in Vancouver, she made a dramatic conversion after a phone call to Secretary Baldrige of the Department of Commerce in the United States, and the Government caved in and decided to pursue a final 15 per cent agreement. That agreement was reached at the end of December.
It is interesting to note that the Minister for International Trade was not even in Washington negotiating but was off on a holiday, apparently in Hawaii, while the civil servants struggled to negotiate this agreement. Most of the editorial writers across the country caught the spirit of that, perhaps none as much as the Toronto Star which is a great newspaper

in the City of Toronto. I believe that editorial of January 7 captured the feelings of many Canadians. It states:
One can only presume that, before she fled to Hawaii, International Trade Minister, Pat Carney-

The other adverse effect of this 15 per cent export tax is that it is imposed on an ad valorem basis. That is that the transportation cost is not taken into account and the transportation cost is the big advantage we have in Ontario because we are relatively closer to the large American markets. In December and January we had a number of shifts in our mills shut down. The Eddy Forest Products plant at Nairn employs about 300 people. The mill at Searchmont was shut down for seven weeks. There were layoffs in various shifts at the mill at Dubreuilville, Ontario. If they pay a fee, they pay it to their band council. Surely, that is within the family of the Indian band. The deal which has been negotiated will end up costing all consumers, both export and domestic customers, something in the neighbourhood of $870 million. That is all part of the deal, which is why the lumber companies are concerned. When the deal is transferred into a stumpage charge, as has been proposed by the Government, instead of being $600 million it will amount to close to $870 million. This will raise the price of Canadian softwood lumber to all customers, including Pacific Rim customers, the European market, as well as domestic customers. speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: SOFTWOOD LUMBER PRODUCTS EXPORT CHARGE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in participating in this debate, perhaps not as much as the Minister of State for Science and Technology, but as a Member of Parliament from a lumber region in British Columbia which is perhaps the most important and most concentrated region to be affected by what we are doing here. It will also be affected by the events that have occurred over the last while as this problem re-emerged.
At the outset, I wish to make three brief points and then discharge them. One, if there was ever a case for the development of a comprehensive free trade agreement with the United States, this is the case.
May I make the analogy with the Auto Pact. Lumber has always been traded freely, and obviously it will not be in the future. If the Auto Pact was good for Ontario, and particular regions of Ontario, a free trade agreement involving lumber would be good for British Columbia, and for other regions. Knowing the benefits of the arrangement, be it sectorial as the Auto Pact is with the United States that provides regulated and free access of Canadian manufactured products, I cannot understand why the Premier of Ontario would stand in the way of other regions in Canada enjoying the same sense of security and benefits that flow from the type of arrangements that we are pursuing with the United States. That is point one. If there was ever a case for free trade, this is it.
Point two has to do with the sovereignty question. My friend and colleague, the Hon. Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) spoke this morning, and surely, together with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), she put this question to bed. If there was ever a case of a red herring, that was it. There is no sovereignty question involved in the settlement that we managed to arrive at with the United States.
Point three deals with the settlement. Of course this is not the way we would have liked this issue to evolve. It would have been great if the tribunal, as it did in 1983, had decided that the Americans have no case against Canada, that it should be discharged from the agenda, and that we would be clear and free. That is not the case. We knew that there would be an
imposition of some duty, be it 15, 20, or 36 per cent, as the Pacific northwest producers were demanding. We knew that it was in the best interest to negotiate. The provinces asked us to negotiate, the responsible portions of the industries that knew what we were heading for and knew what would happen if we had to appeal to GATT suggested the mandate for us was that we enter into negotiation with the United States. Considering the options that were available to us, we arrived at the best possible deal.
The point I wish to make, Sir, and I know that I will be proven right eventually, is that there is a silver lining to this cloud. There is a disguised blessing here. The blessing is that the Americans may well have forced us to do in Canada what we, as politicians in the provinces, and to a lesser extent the federal Government, did not have the political courage and foresight to do ourselves; that is, to raise enough money in the form of economic rent, or from the harvest and the sale of the resource to make sure that in perpetuity we have a stable supply of this precious green gold that grows in every province and is so important to our economic well-being. Lumber and wood fibres are still the major and the main revenue source in terms of export earnings.
As you know, in 1979 I published a paper called "The Green Ghetto". Strangely enough, in 1979 I then defined $300 million as what it would have taken to make the adjustment from the farming mode of our forests to the intensive management regime that is in place in the United States, Sweden, and other countries. We now have that much money. The Americans have forced us to collect that money. We are obligated to pass that money through to the provinces.
If I may leave a message with my provincial colleagues and counterparts who are as foresighted as we are here, I would say to them to use that money wisely, and let us do some of the exciting things that we could do to create many new jobs, give us the stability and certainty that would enable us to pass on to future generations this great and precious resource with which we are so richly blessed.
These are the three points that I wished to introduce. I wish to come back to the last point a little later.
I have always made it a practice in my previous career to look fairly on both sides of an argument and an issue. I learned early in life that it is always good to know your adversary's position. As I said earlier, lumber has always been traded without restriction between Canada and the United States. However, in later years, and perhaps because of our dependence upon that particular industry for economic growth, our industry became increasingly more efficient.
There were several factors which brought this about, not the least of which was the fact that, since 95 per cent of timber in Canada was publicly owned, we were able to provide our private sector mills with the resource at a lesser economic rent than what private sector owners in the United States and other

countries had to charge. I readily admit, having been in the industry myself, that there may have been an advantage to Canadian producers. The Americans may argue that that is a subsidy, but I say: "No". The sovereignty question enters into it, that we shall not be dictated to by anyone outside the country with regard to the value we attach to our natural resources. However, there were other factors.
The Canadian dollar decreased in value in comparison with the U.S. dollar from $1.04 to 73 cents, which is its present value. Perhaps that is the most important and most salient factor in the whole argument. Our industry has a 30 per cent advantage in the exchange rate before our competitors in the Pacific northwest and in other lumber regions in the United States even go to work in the morning. Our industry prudently invested some of this money in modernizing our mills, making incredible gains in efficiency, to the point where we, particularly in the part of Canada which I represent, now have some of the world's most efficient and productive sawmills. We are competitive anywhere, but particularly in the regions of the Pacific northwest and other lumber regions in the United States.
I have travelled through these regions and I have witnessed the devasation of mill closures. They are as difficult in the United States as they are here. I spoke with my friends in the U.S. Senate whom I met over the years. I understand the political reality which they had to face in the United States. I knew in 1983 that this question was not resolved. I knew that it would come back to haunt us because our industry was not prudent enough at that time to read the signals and to put voluntary curbs on their shipments. We were cutting more timber than we ever did before, we were turning out more lumber than we ever did before, and we were getting less money for it because we were driving down the price.
What do the Americans want? They talk about a level playing field, but the playing field has never been level. Let us look at the argument about the need for a different management regime. If we look at the Province of British Columbia today, there are still large areas of virgin timber which have never been touched. There are even some isolated areas to which we do not have any access. There are some timber stands to which there will never be access by road; they will have to be harvested from the air.
In order to manage the resource properly, intelligently, and prudently, one would want to integrate these virgin timber areas into a total management regime. Unlike some people who are less informed about this important industry and its resource, a tree does not grow to heaven. It is a living thing-it is born, it puts down roots, it grows, it matures, and it dies. There is a finite rate of growth even to a tree. It does not grow to heaven. When it matures and dies, it becomes a hazard to nature because it is subject to lightning and fire. We know how the evolutionary chain goes.
There are large areas of timber which is over mature, dead, and no longer commercially viable in British Columbia, as perhaps there are in other provinces. It is a burden because

some of it is on prime land and to clear out the timber to make room for new growth is very costly. Thus a province or a manager of the resource would have to integrate these virgin stands into the total management regime. In order to do that in some cases roads must be built and they must go into remote areas. Therefore we said to the companies: "If you go in there and harvest this over mature timber before it dies and rots on us, we will give you a lesser stumpage". That is only prudent.
In turn, the Americans are harvesting third generation timber. First, they are not getting the same yield and, second, it costs more to grow second and third growth timber over the years. As well, the management of it is entirely different than the management of a virgin resource. That is an important point which the Americans have failed to understand, even though we have tried to make that argument repeatedly. It is not and has not been a level playing field, but it will be.
The Americans should have let us muddle along for another 30 years or 40 years, at which time we would have run out of timber in some prime forest areas in Canada, and the competitive factor would have been much less.
What do the Americans want? The American companies want and need an increase in price to be viable, and the imposition of this tax on Canadian lumber would bring about an increase in price. In the few days the tax has been in place there has already been a marked increase in price in the United States, so the American consumer is really paying the tax. However, we have to pass it through to the companies. It will be a very difficult adjustment but, as I said earlier, an adjustment which has a silver lining to it.
The Americans made the argument that our stumpage appraisal system and other techniques to manage our resource and to ask industry to convert the resource to economic rent and to social benefits was a subsidy. At the same time as the dollar was at 73 cents, our market share in the United States went from 19 per cent to 34 per cent, where it is today.
I knew that we would be in deep trouble if we did not respond to it by finding some way to slow down, either voluntarily or otherwise, and perhaps develop better markets in the Asian countries or in Europe. Mr. Speaker, I have a great deal more faith in your watch than the watch of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade (Mr. McDermid).
I am very pleased to have this opportunity to speak on Bill C-37 because I believe it is an extremely important Bill, not only for what it brings forward in its contents but for its ramifications and what it is going to mean to this country if it is passed. I think this is a very bad Bill. The idea of the Bill is bad. What it is going to do to Canada's negotiating powers in the future I think will be even more detrimental than the detrimental contents of the Bill itself.
This whole idea of reducing and giving away Canada's sovereignty to the United States started in an ill-conceived speech in December to the Economic Club in New York. That was over two years ago. At that time the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that Canada is open for business. In reply the Leader of the Opposition said: "It may be open for business but Canada is not for sale". These were very prophetic words, because what we are seeing now is Canada and Canadians for sale. The interests and heritage of Canadians are for sale.
This particular Memorandum of Understanding which was signed, and which brought about Bill C-37, is a very bad document. It was badly negotiated and badly thought out. Its principle is just horrible. It started primarily on December 30,
Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act
1986 when the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) made her first final offer to the United States to settle the dispute by raising provincial stumpage fees by 10 per cent. This was turned down by the United States. She made a second final offer on November 26 when she suggested there be imposed a 15 per cent export tax on Canadian softwood. However, this offer was rejected by the United States. On December 12 the United States made a counter-offer and the Minister for International Trade rejected it because she said if it was accepted the United States would be able to manage Canadian resources. Yet on December 30 the United States accepted an offer of 15 per cent and that is exactly what it is doing, managing Canadian resources.
This is a very, very sad commentary. It reveals that the Canadian delegation was very poorly prepared. In fact, a report shows that there is a strong rebound in the price of the lumber industry's products and that the financial condition of this industry improved during 1985-86. This is not something which was taken into consideration by the Canadian delegation. However, it was something taken into consideration by the American delegation which decided it would accept the 15 per cent offer from Canada because, if it did go any further, the improved condition of the American forest industry would be a detrimental position for it as far as the arbitration and settling of this situation is concerned.
What also has happened, in addition to the poor economic deal, the Government has created a very bad and detrimental precedent for the future of this country. It has given away the right to negotiate the price for its own resources. Certainly Canada will negotiate prices. It will negotiate the care and control of its own resources. However, here the precedent is that it has allowed the United States to dictate the prices for Canadian resources.
The Government is saying that this is the best deal it could possibly get. This is the deal that it accepted with the gun to its head. This is not a negotiation. This is a fire sale of Canadian resources and the interests of Canadians.
What is going to happen? Canadians do not believe that this deal is going to be beneficial to Canada. Certainly, Canadians do not believe that this precedent is going to do anything but harm to the future economic possibilities and aspirations of this country.
What is happening now is that the Minister is going to embark upon a $12 million advertisement campaign to try to force this deal down the throats of Canadians, to try to gloss with smoke and mirrors and pretty pictures the catastrophe which looms in before the softwood lumber industry and other industries if this precedent is followed, as I am afraid it may be.
What is going to happen? Canadians are not going to be fooled. This deal is going to continue to rebound in the face of the Government and in the face of Canadians. What kind of Government would force this upon Canadians? The aspects,

the eventualities which will happen in the future to this country have not been taken into consideration.
We have a 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber. There is no allowance made in this agreement for a change in the difference between the Canadian and American dollar. If the Canadian dollar goes up vis-a-vis the American dollar this will just be devastating, wiping out a great many of our lumber producers in Canada, even more than will be wiped out by the agreement entered into and agreed to by by this Government. So there are many aspects to consider.
The Minister of State has called Clause 5a of the agreement the sovereignty clause because it provides the following:
The Government of Canada may reduce or eliminate the export charge on the basis of increased stumpage or other charges by provinces on softwood lumber production.
Yet Clause 2(3) of the Bill which is now before us states that the Memorandum of Understanding may be referred to in interpreting this Bill. This establishes that the Minister's sovereignty claim is not correct. In fact, Clause 5b of the agreement provides:
Calculation of the value of any replacement measures in relation to the export charge will be subject to further consultations and agreement between the two Governments.
The Government would have us believe that this export charge, presumably to be used by the federal Government and the provincial Governments, will go back into the lumber industry. The Americans have another idea with respect to the agreement. They do not for one minute expect that this money will go back into the industry. In fact, if it does go back into the industry they will consider it a breach of the agreement.
Clause 6 of the Memorandum of Understanding provides:
The Government of Canada will take no action, and will take all reasonable steps to ensure that no other governmental body in Canada takes any action, directly or indirectly, which has the effect of offsetting or reducing the export charge or replacement measures-
President Reagan has pledged in writing that he will take action if Canada does not live up to the terms of the agreement. Attached to the Memorandum of Understanding dated December 30 is a letter addressed to the Coalition for Fair Lumber Imports. In that letter U.S. Secretary of Commerce Malcolm Baldrige identifies seven different types of Canadian government assistance to industry which the U.S. will not accept. These include rebate, remission, deferral of the export charge, provision of grants or low-cost loans, exemption from other federal and provincial government charges, assumption of obligations currently borne by the industry, reduction in stumpage or other fees, changes in the way that the volume of timber harvest is measured, and the non-competitive awarding of contracts for silviculture, road-building, recreational and other forestry activities. This is something from which we will come away empty-handed.
I think that the only point the Government can make is that if we are to lose 15 per cent it is better that it remain in
Canadian hands as opposed to American hands. But that is the only point that the Government can possibly make.
So what are we giving up? First, we are giving up something that we probably need not have had to pay. We are giving up something that the economic indicators in the United States tell us is something that is not necessary because the lumber industry there is healthy, and getting healthier all the time. While it may regress later on, at this point in time it is getting healthier. That strengthens the Canadian position, but it is not something which the Canadians took into consideration in their haste to sign this Memorandum of Understanding.
Second, if there is a change in the American-Canadian dollar ratio, and if the Canadian dollar improves with respect to the American dollar then this measure will become even more detrimental to Canada.
Third, we are selling future relations and negotiations with the United States down the river as a result of entering into this agreement, not to mention the fourth point which is what it will do to the lumber industry in Canada. It has been stated by Bob Rivard of the Canadian Lumbermen's Assocation that lumber production could drop by as much as 25 per cent in 1987. The Government of Canada continues to insist that the provinces can use their share of the export charge revenue as they see fit. There will be a very interesting session of meetings between the federal Government and the provincial Governments. If the provincial Governments buy this federal government line I will be very surprised.
Fifth, what will this measure do to Canada's relations in the GATT? How can Canada now say that what the United States is doing to our country is wrong when Canada directly and blatantly violated the principles of GATT by entering into this Memorandum of Understanding with the United States? This is the first time that we have imposed a tax on trade with only one of our trading partners, which violates the first principle of international trade. What we have done is we have said: "United States, you can negotiate with us and enter into our business. You can pass judgment on our laws and regulations. If something hurts you, then you can hold us up at the border by threatening a countervailing tariff or an import charge and we will just knuckle under". Why should the Americans not believe this when we have given them every reason even before this to believe it? We did away with FIRA.
In the negotiations with the United States we were blatantly told what should and should not be included. The Government said that there would not be countervailing sanctions or tariffs on Canadian products. The Government said that the United States would not do that. Yet what happened? It has been doing it ever since. The way in which the Government has handled these negotiations amounts to nothing more than waving a big red flag in front of the American lobby organizations. By saying that we want free trade with the United States we have alarmed all the lobby organizations which have run to Washington to talk to their representatives and their Congressmen. What we have done is we have firmed up the position of

the industry in the United States by ensuring that Canadian imports and Canadian products will never be a threat again.
The softwood lumber case is not the only case to consider. I refer Hon. Members to the recent ruling of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in the United States with respect to the sale of natural gas from Canadian producers to American buyers. The way the situation has worked in the past is that Canadian producers enter into agreements with American buyers. Included in these agreements is a clause with respect to a charge for transportation through the Canadian pipeline system. That charge is passed along to the purchasers in the United States. This arrangement is set out in the agreements and agreed to by the National Energy Board, which is the Canadian regulatory body. On December 3 the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in the United States said: "No. You cannot do that. Canadian natural gas is becoming too competitive". We are hearing this from the same country which three years ago said that we had to get rid of the National Energy Program and treat Americans the same as Canadians. They told us that we could not show bias to Canadians, that we had to open up our oil and gas industry to Americans.
What happened? We opened up the industry and they turned on us. I am referring to the same regulatory body which in 1984 outlawed Canadian take-or-pay contracts with the United States. We do away with take or pay contracts. We do it the way the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission wants, we will get a competitive edge on price for a fraction of time and then they change the rules on us again.
Why should they not think that they can change the rules on us again? We have been down on our knees to them for the last two years begging for a free trade agreement, saying that we do not care what it is in the free trade agreement, take what you want, but when we sign it, call it a free trade agreement.
That is not good enough for Canadians, and why should it be? Canadians are the losers. Not only are Canadians losing, but they are being shut out. It is the most one-sided negotiation in the history of Canadian trade. The Government is not saying that there is a tarnishment or a reduction in Canadian sovereignty. It is saying that there is no reduction, there is no imposition on Canadian sovereignty. That is what it is saying to us in the House, but that is not what it is meaning with respect to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission decision.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) when he was in Los Angeles on January 7 said that this decision by the FERC was detrimental to Canada. He stated:
