Mr. Speaker, I wish to participate in this debate because there are no issues more relevant to anyone in Canada, and particularly to people in Atlantic Canada, than trade and forestry. I have followed the debate closely with enthusiasm and great interest, and sometimes with fright and disbelief at the incredible remarks I have heard made by Members opposite. We have heard many statements based on fiction rather than fact. There are many inconsistencies among the Members opposite and, more particularly, among Members peculiar to a particular Party.
This issue must be debated with the general knowledge that Canada is in a very unique position with respect to trade. The difficulty which the Opposition has in presenting its case adequately is another example of the difficulty it has had in making intelligent or constructive comment on any matters relative to trade.
We must bear in mind that Canada is a very unique trading nation. We are more dependent upon trade than is any other country in the western world. One-third of everything we produce goes beyond our borders. We are a nation of only 25 million and are, therefore, more reliant upon trade than any other country. Only 10 per cent of what is produced in the United States is exported. Only 16 per cent of the production of Japan is sold abroad, and only 26 per cent of the produce of the United Kingdom is sold abroad. Therefore, the steps which we must take and the sensitivity which we must have is peculiar to Canada. Strategems which may have guided the destinies of other nations with regard to trade are obviously not appropriate for Canada. In 1970 Canada was the fourth largest trading nation in the world, just ahead of Japan. Today Japan has doubled its exports and Canada is in eighth place.
Some months ago we were hit with a countervail from the United States. That was not only a result of the protests of producers and purchasers of lumber in the United States about our situation with regard to lumber, but was symptomatic of everything that is happening in Canada with respect to trade with the United States. We experienced a series of tariffs, countervails, threats and protectionist legislation on hogs, beef, steel, fish, shakes and shingles, and raspberries. Every commodity of consequence which we have been sending south of the border has been subject to scrutiny, criticism, and attack from the elements there.
We are experiencing an international trade war. The European Common Market seemed unable to control its members who have participated in unfair trade practices. There has been retaliation by the United States. Recently a 200 per cent countervail duty was placed on the European Common Market. There will obviously be a reaction to that from the European Common Market and so on.
Members opposite ask us to ignore the realities of the situation. They say that we should allow the due process of law to proceed and take our chances in the legal and trade forums

January 20, 1987
Adjournment Debate
in the United States and GATT. The realities of the situation compel the conclusion that we would obviously not get a fair hearing. Our destiny was fixed. Therefore, after consulting with all of the provinces and receiving from them an endorsement and encouragement, the federal Government started negotiations with the United States. Those are the realities. My friends in the New Democratic Party must come out of their igloos. We are now in the 20th century. We must turn on the light bulb and become aware of the realities.
Members in that particular Party are against everything. It is about time they took a position with regard to what they are in favour of. I do not encourage them to take the position of the Liberal Party which has so many positions that it does not know where it stands on any issue. I plead with members of the New Democratic Party to tell us what they are in favour of and what position they would have taken in this matter.
If we had done nothing they would have asked why we did not stand up for Canada, why we did not take action to avoid the countervail, why we did not negotiate to minimize our losses when we had the opportunity to do so. Their chief argument, which has been repeated many times, is that we have conceded sovereignty. They say that we have allowed the United States to trespass upon the parameters of Canadian privacy and have, therefore, conceded our inalienable right forever and a day. They say that this is a precedent which will prejudice us forever.
During this debate Members have spoken about the sacrosanct Auto Pact. The Auto Pact is an agreement representing the positions of both countries. Is the Auto Pact a concession of sovereignty? Nay, Mr. Speaker. It is an assertion of sovereignty. When we enter a marriage contract, join a church, a political Party or an association, we assert our right and our sovereignty. We indicate which rights we wish to exercise with agreement and consultation with the other Party.
If the logic of Members opposite is followed, all of the international agreements which we have made throughout history involve a surrender of sovereignty. Obviously, that is not the case. There is no authority in Canada which will stand behind the representations made by Members opposite that our sovereignty has been intruded upon. I defy those Members to find an authority of consequence who would stand behind their position.
We have the money in our hands and we have the authority and discretion to spend that money for the betterment of forestry in Canada. I would like to compliment my colleague, the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew), who has promulgated the difficulties of his Ministry so well in Canada. He deserves the congratulations of this House as does the Minister of International Trade (Miss Carney).
In closing, this is a good deal for Atlantic Canada. It has the endorsement of the Maritime Lumber Bureau. They are saying
enthusiastically and unequivocally that this deal was in the best interest of Canada. They told me that five minutes ago.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NICARAGUA-BOMBING MISSIONS LAUNCHED FROM HONDURAS. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT URGE HONDURAS TO DISARM CONTRA FORCES
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NICARAGUA-BOMBING MISSIONS LAUNCHED FROM HONDURAS. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT URGE HONDURAS TO DISARM CONTRA FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address the question of Canada's relations with Central America. This arises out of a question on Honduras that I put to the Government on December 11.
I asked if the Government would request Honduras to obey international law by ceasing to host the Contra forces attacking Nicaragua, on pain of losing a large amount of economic aid that Canada supplies. On December 15 I received an entirely unsatisfactory letter from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in which he ignored the fact of Honduran support for the war against Nicaragua, but stated that Canadian aid is not "given on the satisfaction of certain political conditions". The Government tries to reduce terrorist attacks and violations of international law to questions of political conditions. The Hon. Minister ought to know that his letter obscures the difference between law and political considerations.
In 1981 Canada suspended bilateral aid to the Government of Guatemala because of its record of grossly tolerating human rights violations. Most Canadian church and non-government organizations informed about conditions in central America favoured that decision, supporting the rule of law, as did my own Party.
The Canadian Government halted Canadian bilateral aid also to El Salvador, again because that Government was tolerating human rights violations. However, Canada has now resumed bilateral aid to that country, claiming that the Duarte Government has substantially improved the human rights situation there. While I and many other informed Canadians believe that decision to be in error, Canada's Government clearly thought it was appropriate to make that decision on grounds the Minister would call political.
I might mention one further case. Canada stopped giving bilateral aid to Cuba on the grounds that it was supplying military aid to Angola, when Angola needed that support to resist external aggression by South Africa.
To claim that such considerations do not enter into decisions to grant or withhold bilateral aid, as the Minister claims, is
January 20, 1987

nonsense. Canadians know that it is nonsense. Honduras is the largest single recipient of Canadian bilateral aid in Central America. As the Minister points out in his letter, that Government has received over $43 million in aid during the period 1982 to 1986. That Government is directly involved in the support of the U.S.-sponsored war of terrorist attacks against the people of Nicaragua. It tolerates the existence of some
14,000	Contra terrorists and mercenaries on its soil. Rather than disarming the Contras, it disposes of its own people, some 800 of whom were evacuated from Contra occupied areas in October alone. It has turned over the Swan Islands off the Atlantic coast and El Tigre in the Gulf of Fonseca to the United States for training and supplying the Contras and for staging attacks on Nicaragua. It provides the Contras with a string of air bases within Honduras, and shares the base at El Agucate with U.S. and Contra forces.
As an apparent consequence of Honduran support for these terrorist attacks, human rights abuses in Honduras are on the increase. In September, 1986, at least 14 men were assassinated. In October, 28 men and women were murdered.
The Minister says that Canada wants to reduce the underlying economic and social causes of tension in Honduras. I say to the Minister that one of the underlying economic and social causes of tension in Honduras is the presence of Contra bases and the support that Honduras is providing for President Reagan's war.
The same could be said of El Salvador. Again, the impossibility of fundamental changes in economic and social structures, and in human rights, is closely linked to the U.S. program of low intensity warfare. El Salvador provides the United States and the Contras with air bases, including the one at Ilopango which has been used to supply Contra invaders in Nicaragua by Hassenfus and his associates. In return, the U.S. supports the strength of the military and right wing elites that, at minimum, prevent Duarte from engaging in fundamental reforms.
The Government may believe that its resumption of bilateral aid to El Salvador has improved human rights there. I say to the Minister that he has yet to convince the Canadian churches and non-governmental organizations that have experience in that sorry country. At this moment, the Government is considering the resumption of bilateral aid to Guatemala. I want to warn the Minister that resumption of bilateral aid at this time threatens to draw Canada into the same trap as in El Salvador and Honduras.
We cannot pretend that bilateral aid has no political or military implications in a war-torn region where everything and everyone is judged by their relationship to the American war. We cannot pretend to alleviate human rights violations by supporting governments which exist at the mercy of those military and economic interests which oppose basic economic and social change. We must remember that the U.S. doctrine of low intensity conflict calls for mixtures of military and
Adjournment Debate
economic or so-called humanitarian aid to support repressive local elites.
It is time this Government issued a clear call to the Government of Honduras to cease and desist its support for the Contras. It is time we went beyond words and took action. The largest single recipient of Canadian aid in Central America should not be the primary base for U.S. terrorism in that region, which Honduras is. Instead, we should direct Canadian aid away from that country to a country where, in the opinion of many of the churches and non-governmental organizations with first-hand experience in the region, it would do the most good. At present, that country is Nicaragua which is vigorously struggling to rebuild its education, agriculture, housing, health care and all the arts of peace. The very first step we should take, which would use only 10 per cent of what we are now wasting in Honduras, is to open an embassy in the capital of Nicaragua, Managua.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NICARAGUA-BOMBING MISSIONS LAUNCHED FROM HONDURAS. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT URGE HONDURAS TO DISARM CONTRA FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as he was told by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in the letter dated December 15 last, the Hon. Member knows that Canada has clearly come out in favour of a pacific settlement of the current crisis in Central America. We are opposed to the intervention of a third party anywhere in that region, and we deplore the inclusion of Central America in the East-West dispute and the militarization of that region.
Canada is against the supply of weapons to the opposing factions of the region. The Honduran Government has proven to be moderate despite the difficult situation it has been put in by the presence of Contras and, more or less successfully, it has tried not to intervene militarily in the dispute. Apparently the Hondurans have formally requested that the Contra forces leave their territory. We are concerned about the raids made in Honduras by the Sandinistan soldiers in pursuit of Contras because this can only exacerbate existing tensions. It would be unrealistic to think, as the Hon. Member has suggested, that Honduras could act unilaterally and disarm the Contras which now have almost as many troops as it has. We hope that the problems created by the presence of insurgents in Central America will be solved through national and regional reconciliation efforts.
Canada has joined international initiatives to promote a regional peace plan by voicing strong support for the Contadora process and indicating its willingness to play a constructive role whenever it will be practical and appropriate. At the request of the Contadora group countries, we have conveyed our observations on the security and control measures contained in the proposed Contadora Act. The Secretary of State on January 18, 1987, reiterated Canada's support to the Contadora process in a message to the Foreign Affairs Ministers of the countries involved in the Contadora group and in the Lima Support Group, as well as to the Secretaries General of the United Nations Organization and the Organization of American States at a time when they are initiating a

January 20, 1987
Adjournment Debate
tour of the area to consider the prospects of a resumption of negotiations. The Minister was pleased with the Contadora group's latest initiative. The Government of Canada for its part feels that today more than ever, it is important that the process go on because it could help reduce tensions in the area and provide the framework for a possible solution.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION-ACTION TAKEN BY IMMIGRATION APPEAL BOARD
IMMIGRATION-ACTION TAKEN BY IMMIGRATION APPEAL BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before Christmas the people of the lower mainland of British Columbia became aware that the Immigration Appeal Board in Vancouver a year previous had prevented the deportation of Mr. John Michael Lewis from Canada. He was a convicted child molester. He landed in Canada in 1981 and was already wanted in Utah and California on outstanding 1980 and 1982 charges involving sexual exploitation of minors. He had already served a jail term in B.C. for sex offences with boys. He has been allowed to stay in Canada since 1985 when the Board stayed a deportation order against him.
I guess what infuriates the public, and certainly what infuriates me, is the fact that there are literally hundreds of thousands of people from around the world who want to come into Canada simply to enjoy the good life and provide for their families. These are people who want to live quiet and peaceful lives and who will never violate the law. Yet the Immigration Appeal Board goes out of its way to spend its concern for somebody who is a felon, someone who has been convicted of a criminal offense. There is no accounting for it. It violates the sense of rightness in society. It violates the values in society. It possibly exposes the children of our society to danger since it seems that this man had a proclivity to children. There is no excuse for it.
The Immigration Act, 1976, in Section 19 outlines the inadmissible classes and states:
(1) No person shall be granted admission if he is a member of any of the
following classes:
(c) persons who have been convicted of an offence that, if committed in Canada, constitutes or, if committed outside Canada, would constitute an offence that may be punishable under any Act of Parliament and for which a maximum term of imprisonment of ten years or more may be imposed-
Mr. Lewis falls into an inadmissible class. The Act goes on to state the following in Section 21:
Where a removal order is made against any person with respect to whom an inquiry is held as a result of a report made pursuant to subsection 20(1), the removal order against that person may be made on the basis that that person is a member of any inadmissible class.
I want to know why the Immigration Appeal Board, which was appointed by the previous Government I might add, ruled as it did in this case. I wish to give credit where credit is due and point out that one member of the Board was the former Leader of the Liberal Party in British Columbia. He voted
against this application. It is the other two who are the guilty ones.
In the House before Christmas I asked if it would be possible to bring these Immigration Appeal Board people to justice for violating the law of Canada. I took the trouble to look at the oath of office which they take. I have never seen such an insipid, milquetoast oath that anyone has to take. It is clear that on that type of an oath they can do anything they want. They are not even asked to swear to uphold the law of Canada. I say to the Minister that it is time we looked at the oath of office so that those who sit on these appeal boards and adjudicate have at least to take an oath of office to uphold the law of Canada, as they did not do in this case.
I seek an assurance from the Minister that he will pursue the appeal about which he spoke in the House and that he will re-evaluate the process under which the immigration appeal system works and that the oath of office will change to make these people uphold the law of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: IMMIGRATION-ACTION TAKEN BY IMMIGRATION APPEAL BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to expand on the reply given by the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) to the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) on December 16, 1986. I have a great deal of respect for the judgment of the Hon. Member and am very conscious of his concern with respect to this matter.
Where a permanent resident is ordered deported he may appeal that order to the Immigration Appeal Board. The Board has sole and exclusive jurisdiction to decide upon such matters, subject only to appeal on a question of law or jurisdiction to the Federal Court of Canada. There cannot be any political interference by the Government in these decisions of an independent judicial body.
In November, 1984, the Board exercised its lawful discretion and stayed the execution of the deportation order, subject to review in February, 1989, or at such earlier date as determined by the Board. Based on suspected non-compliance of the terms and conditions set by the Board when its decision was reached, a motion to review was filed by Immigration officials requesting that the Board reconsider its original decision. This motion was dismissed on December 5, 1986, as the Board was not satisfied that Mr, Lewis had failed to comply with its terms and conditions. The Department has therefore initiated action in the Federal Court of Canada challenging the Board's decision.

subtopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-(A) ALGONQUIN RADIO OBSERVATORY (B) PROFESSIONALS' FUTURE PROSPECTS

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-(A) ALGONQUIN RADIO OBSERVATORY (B) PROFESSIONALS' FUTURE PROSPECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 3, 1986, I asked a question in this House concerning the Algonquin Radio Observatory, a project that came under the National Research Council, and I asked the
January 20, 1987

Minister of Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) whether the Government had in fact made the decision, as reported by certain newspapers, to close that radio observatory.
The Minister answered he was not quite sure, that he did not know whether the report would be confirmed and, as far as he was concerned, if a decision had been made, it had been by the National Research Council rather than by the Government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the matter of research and development is of concern to me and to many Members in this House. I for one believe that research and development do create jobs in Canada and that we will go on being provided with that means of remaining competitive on international markets.
But the closing down of that radio observatory does not involve jobs only-there is also the whole matter of increased efforts by the scientific world to try and get from this Government funding and concrete support for research and development.
Mr. Speaker, I am not alone in sounding the alarm, in stating that the Government is slashing, cutting, reducing research and development funding. At the National Research Council, and the Committee got it straight from the President himself, some $60 million was cut in this year's budget, and further similar cuts are expected in order to transfer funds to the so-called space agency that is supposed to be set up shortly.
Mr. Speaker, during the holidays I was reading some newspaper articles on the subject of where we are headed in the science and technology sector. I clipped an article in Le Droit by Dexter, an editorial writer, who wrote on January 6 of this year, and 1 quote:
The Government in Ottawa and pure research, a shocking state of affairs.
He went on to say:
The Government in Ottawa is threatening our pure research sector by treating the National Research Council of Canada like a business. When Brian Mulroney poses for the camera and hands a cheque for $1 million to Rick Hansen, while NRC researchers get their pink slip, we see the sad spectacle of a head of state who has no understanding of the role of pure research in a society's maturing process.
Mr. Speaker, it was the Conservative Government that made the cut in the NRC budget. It is going to divert these monies to the private sector and to the creation of a Canadian space agency. This proves how inconsistent the Government is. Perhaps I may recall certain facts that will show how shortsighted this Government is, its total lack of vision and lack of any consistent policy.
The latest research and development effort undertaken since the NASA program is without a doubt the new research program dubbed Star Wars. The U.S. Administration has asked the Canadian Government whether it wanted to be associated with the project, and the Canadian Government said no, we are not interested. I can't blame it for that. It exercised its right as a Government to make that decision.
However, ever since the Conservatives came to power, more than $120 million have been cut from the NRC budget. The last cuts totalling $20 million, announced last October, will
Adjournment Debate
oblige the NRC to cut between 100 and 150 jobs. The Minister has announced a project worth $1 billion in investments, but this amount will come not from investments, but from commitments from the private sector if everything goes well. This is not new money, but promises.
The Conservative Government has announced the creation of a space agency which will take part in the manned orbiting station project of NASA. We refused to take part in the Star Wars program, but as we all know, there are rumors that we shall join the Pentagon for a space station project which will eventually be used for Star Wars. This is not really consistent or logical, but what can you expect?
Canada will therefore take part indirectly in Star Wars because it will take part in the space station project.
The Government is not being very farsighted in this affair, Mr. Speaker. We deserve some explanation and I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to clarify this issue. For my part, I do not understand how we can say no to Star Wars while taking part in the space agency project.
If we seriously want to do research in electronics and microelectronics, we shall have to do so through recognized scientific organizations such as the National Research Council.
In closing, as my allotted time is about to expire, I would like to say that I do not object to the proposed space agency. On the contrary, I believe that it should be integrated with the National Research Council, which has the capability to provide the necessary expertise and which has facilities here, in Ottawa. So I hope that the decision to set up this space program will be translated into a real Government objective, that it will be implemented, and that the National Research Council will be asked to play a leading role. Once the necessary and adequate funding has been provided by the Government, we might have a better research and development program, more jobs, more stable employment, more competition at the international level, and perhaps better Canadian products.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL-(A) ALGONQUIN RADIO OBSERVATORY (B) PROFESSIONALS' FUTURE PROSPECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to reply to the Hon. Member's original question where he asked the Minister to explain what was happening with the Algonquin Radio Observatory. For some reason there is much misinformation and concern in respect of this particular item, and I welcome this chance to set the record straight.
NRC's mandate includes the responsiblity to "operate and administer any astronomical observatories established or maintained by the Government of Canada". At present, NRC runs three facilities-radio telescopes in Algonquin and Penticton, and an optical telescope and computation centre in Victoria. NRC also contributes to the Canada-France-Hawaii optical telescope in Mauna Kea, Hawaii, gaining thereby 40

January 20, 1987
Adjournment Debate
per cent of the operating time. These instruments are heavily used by university researchers from Canada and other countries. As well, NRC has many fine astronomers in its own right.
The Algonquin Radio Observatory consists of three instruments-a 46 metre fully steerable parabolic reflector, a compound solar interferometer and a small solar radio telescope. The large reflector was constructed over 20 years ago and needs major refurbishment so that it can operate at millimeter wavelengths. This reflector is also expensive to operate and some astronomers question the cost-benefit payoff from continuing to use the telescope as is.
Since an initial decision to proceed, the estimated cost of the refurbishment rose from $7.9 million to $11.7 million. In view of this, plans to refurbish the telescope have been cancelled. In the words of Dr. Kerwin, "We do not have the money and therefore we cannot resurface and therefore it becomes obsolete". The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) had no role in directing the reductions toward the Algonquin Radio Observatory. NRC management took that decision.
As of now, no other decisions have been made. The facility will operate this winter, and further decisions may be made next summer. In addition, the NRC task group is reviewing NRC's decision on the telescope right now.
NRC, in consultation with Canadian astronomers, is looking at a variety of options for the Algonquin Radio Observatory. They want to give Canadians access to the best possible facilities within budget constraints. Alternative sources of funding are being sought which would permit the telescope to be operated at less cost to NRC. Ways of strengthing other facilities are being looked at so that some of the same services can be provided elsewhere. Finally, NRC is looking into obtaining increased access to existing observatories.
It is not a pleasant task to have to review existing operations and re-allocate resources. Nevertheless, if federal research efforts are to be focused on agreed priorities, priorities which have emerged after long and careful thought by all interested parties, then the issue must be faced squarely and appropriate decisions taken.
